title: extensions/
body:
extensions/ An extension adds to BxAgents without changing it: chat commands ( /deploy , /roll 2d6 ), listeners for the events of the chat and of bx-ai, and schedules that run when the agent is served. It is a class that looks and behaves like a ColdBox ModuleConfig : it has a configure() , an onLoad() and an onUnload() , its settings come from Agent.yaml , and things are handed to it with $inject . One file is a whole extension: extensions/ hello.bx /hello roll.bx /roll, /coin standup/ a folder is an extension too Extension.bx commands/Standup.bx schedulers/Reminder.bx A working project with all of these is examples/extensions-agent . The smallest extension extensions/hello.bx . The file name is the extension's name. class { function configure() { variables.settings = { greeting : "Hello" } } @Command( "hello" ) @Hint( "say hello: /hello " ) function greet( agentContext, commandArguments ) { return agentContext.reply().ok( "#settings.greeting#, #commandArguments#!" ) } } Run bxAgents chat and type /hello Ada . /extensions lists what is loaded. A command method is called with the agentContext (the conversation and nothing else; the same object the built-in commands get) and the text after the command name. It returns a Reply ( agentContext.reply().ok( "..." ) , .warn() , .keyValues() , .grid() , .choose() ) or just a string. If it throws, the person sees a warning that names the extension and the chat carries on. Annotations Annotations are normal BoxLang annotations on a method. Each one can be written four ways, and every BxAgents annotation takes all four: Written Means Example bare defaults; the name comes from the method @Command on function roll() is /roll simple the main value @Command( "deploy" ) array several @Alias( [ "dice", "d" ] ) struct every option @Command( { name : "deploy", hint : "plan it", admin : true, aliases : [ "ship" ], transports : [ "tui", "web" ] } ) Shorthand annotations say one option each: @Hint( "..." ) , @Admin , @Alias( ... ) , @Transports( [ "tui", "web" ] ) . A struct option wins over a shorthand, and the clash is shown in /extensions . Annotation names ignore case. transports are where the command runs: tui (the terminal chat), web (the web page and the HTTP command route) and gateway (chat platforms). The default is all three. A chat platform only answers the commands its gateway allows ( gatewaySession.commands.allow ), and a command with @Admin only runs for the people listed as admins there. Settings The extension says its defaults in configure() , as a module does: function configure() { variables.settings = { target : "staging", environments : [ "staging", "production" ] } } The people who use it change them under the extension's name in Agent.yaml : extensions: deploy: target: production A person can set their own values in ~/.bxagents/bxAgents.yml (same extensions: block); the project's values win over theirs. Nested structs merge key by key, arrays and simple values replace. In the extension, settings is the merged struct. Lifecycle Method When configure() once, first. Sets variables.settings . No work here onLoad() after the settings are merged and everything is injected. Open connections, start timers onUnload() when the chat or the server ends. Release them this.title , this.author , this.webURL , this.description , this.version and this.enabled are read as in a module config, and this.dependencies = [ "other-extension" ] loads that extension first. An extension that throws while it loads is shown as failed in /extensions with the reason; the others still load. Injection Every class of an extension has $inject( name, object )`. It puts the object in both the `this` and the `variables` scopes. For private only: `$inject( name, object, "variables" ) . $read( name ) reads a variables entry from outside. BxAgents injects two things before onLoad() : settings and log ( log.info( "..." ) , .warn() , .error() ; what an extension logs is also in /extensions ). To share an object between the files of an extension, create it in onLoad() and $inject it where it is needed. The same call is how a test hands an extension a fake. A folder extension A folder has the same shape as an agent project: extensions/standup/ Extension.bx optional: the module config (properties, configure(), onLoad(), onUnload()) commands/ one class per command, like the built-in ones schedulers/ BoxLang scheduler classes, started when the agent is served A class in commands/ extends models.chat.commands.BaseCommand@bxagents and says its name() , hint() , transports() and run( context, args ) . settings and log are injected into it. Schedulers A class in schedulers/ is a BoxLang scheduler : a class with a configure() that defines tasks through the scheduler property BoxLang gives it, like any other BoxLang scheduler. When the agent is served ( bxAgents serve , a .bxa , a deployed server) it starts in the runtime's scheduler service. Like every class of an extension it is given settings (the defaults with the values from Agent.yaml ) and log before configure() runs: class { function configure() { scheduler.task( "standup-reminder" ) .call( () => log.info( "Standup time for #settings.channel#" ) ) .everyDayAt( settings.at ) .withNoOverlaps() } } The BoxLang scheduler lifecycle methods ( onStartup() , onShutdown() , onAnyTaskError() and the rest) work as usual. Each scheduler is registered as extension-- , and a scheduler that fails to start is reported on its extension in /extensions while the others still run. The terminal chat does not start schedulers: they belong to the served agent. Listening to events An extension is also an interceptor. A method named after an event listens to it, exactly like a BoxLang or ColdBox interceptor: class { function onChatInput( data ) { if ( data.text contains "password" ) { data.cancel( "That looks like a password, so it was not sent." ) } } function onAIError( data ) { log.warn( "the model failed" ) } } Two things can be listened to: bx-ai events ( beforeAIAgentRun , afterAIModelInvoke , onAIError , beforeAIToolExecute and the rest). They fire wherever the agent runs. Chat events , announced by BxAgents: Event When data has A listener can onChatSessionStart / onChatSessionEnd the terminal chat opens or closes agent , transport onChatInput before a message is sent text , transport cancel( reason ) , or replace( newText ) onChatTurnStart / onChatTurnEnd around one turn of the agent text , transport ( reply , status at the end) onChatConversationChange /new , /resume , /clear , /fork or /compact changed the conversation line , transport onChatCommandBefore before any command, on every transport line , name , arguments , transport cancel( reason ) onChatCommandAfter after any command, on every transport line , name , reply , transport replace( newReply ) The session, input, turn and conversation events are the terminal chat's; the two command events fire in the terminal, the web page and on chat platforms alike. A listener that throws is caught: it can never stop a turn, the listeners after it still run, and the error is shown in /extensions . @On binds a method with another name, or many events at once, and takes the four forms an annotation takes: @On( [ "beforeAIToolExecute", "afterAIToolExecute" ] ) function toolCalled( data ) { log.info( "a tool ran" ) } @On naming an event the runtime does not know is reported in /extensions , not ignored. interceptors and customInterceptionPoints As in a module config, configure() can name classes from the extension's folder to register, each with its own properties, and points of its own to announce: function configure() { variables.interceptors = [ { class : "interceptors.Audit", properties : { level : "info" } } ] variables.customInterceptionPoints = [ "onAuditRecorded" ] } interceptors/Audit.bx listens with methods named after events and has settings , log and properties injected. Any extension can then listen to onAuditRecorded , and the one that owns it announces it with BoxAnnounce( "onAuditRecorded", { ... } ) . extensions.disable takes extension:method to turn one listener off. ColdBox events ( preProcess , postProcess and the rest) are not part of the terminal chat; they fire only in a served agent. Keys and status @Key binds keys in the terminal chat to a method. On a command method it runs that command, with the same rules and events as typing it; on any other method it calls the method with the agentContext and an empty text and shows what it returns. @Hint (or hint in the struct form) says what it does. @Command @Hint( "count a pulse" ) @Key( "ctrl+g" ) function pulse( agentContext, commandArguments ) { ... } @Key( { keys : [ "ctrl+y", "alt+y" ], hint : "reset the count" } ) function resetPulse( agentContext, commandArguments ) { ... } A key is named extension:method ( pulse:pulse ). /keys lists it with the built-in ones, and a person can give it other keys under chat: keys: in ~/.bxagents/bxAgents.yml . A key a built-in action already uses, or an earlier extension holds, is refused with a sentence that says so. A typed draft stays in the box while a key runs. Keys are for the terminal chat; the web page and chat platforms have commands. @Status is a piece of status next to the size of the context: a method that returns a short text, asked each time the box is drawn in the terminal and after each change to the conversation on the web page (small chips in the header). Return an empty string to show nothing. It must be quick; one that throws is left out and the reason is put on its extension once. @Status function beats( agentContext ) { return variables.beats > 0 ? "beat #variables.beats#" : "" } extensions.disable takes extension:method for a key or a status item too. register( registry ) What annotations cannot say, because it is worked out in code, is said as calls. If the class has a register( registry ) method it is called once, right after configure() : function register( registry ) { registry.command( "deploy", { run : ( agentContext, commandArguments ) => ..., hint : "ship it", admin : true, aliases : [ "ship" ] } ) registry.key( "ctrl+d", "/deploy", { hint : "ship it" } ) // a key that runs a command line registry.key( "ctrl+o", ( agentContext ) => "opened", { name : "open", hint : "open it" } ) // or any function registry.status( "branch", ( agentContext ) => "main" ) registry.on( "onChatCommandAfter", ( data ) => ... ) // an event, or an array of them } Prefixes and @ sources Both are for the terminal chat only. @Prefix claims the start of a line in the message box. The method gets the agentContext and the text after the prefix. It answers one of two ways: a Reply (or a string) is shown and nothing is sent, and { send : "text" } is sent to the agent as the message, after onChatInput has seen it. @Prefix( "%" ) @Hint( "ask for an explanation: % why is the sky blue" ) function explain( agentContext, text ) { return { send : "Explain this in one short paragraph: #text#" } } @Prefix( "=" ) function count( agentContext, text ) { return agentContext.reply().ok( "#text.listToArray( ' ' ).len()# words" ) } / , ! , # and @ are the chat's own, and a lone ? asks for the keys; a prefix that starts with one of them, is empty or has a space is refused with a sentence. The longest prefix wins. Two extensions on one prefix are a warning and the later layer wins. @Source( "ticket" ) brings content along with a message the way @path brings a file. Write @ticket:TCK-1 (or @ticket:"two words" ) and the method is called with the agentContext and the query. It returns { name, content } , an array of them or a string; the content goes with the message and the mention stays in it. @Suggest( "ticket" ) on another method is optional: it returns the values the menu offers as the person types after the colon. It is asked on keystrokes, so it must be quick; one that throws gives no suggestions and the reason is put on its extension once. A source name can be anything that starts with a letter, since files are plain @path . @Source( "ticket" ) function ticket( agentContext, query ) { return { name : "ticket #query#", content : tickets[ query ] } } @Suggest( "ticket" ) function ticketNames( agentContext, query ) { return tickets.keyArray() } Written as calls: registry.prefix( "%", ( agentContext, text ) => ..., { hint : "..." } ) and registry.source( "ticket", ( agentContext, query ) => ..., { hint : "...", suggest : ( agentContext, query ) => [ ... ] } ) . The person chooses the prefix or the name, by the id extension:method , in ~/.bxagents/bxAgents.yml : chat: prefixes: desk:explain: "?%" sources: desk:ticket: issue A choice that cannot be used is reported and the extension's own is kept. extensions.disable takes extension:method for these too. Asking the person A command, key or prefix can put a question to the person while it runs: var title = agentContext.ask( "Title of the ticket?", { default : commandArguments, help : "A short sentence." } ) var priority = agentContext.choose( "Priority?", [ "low", "normal", { value : "high", label : "high", hint : "someone is blocked" } ] ) if ( agentContext.confirm( "Make the #priority# ticket?" ) ) { ... } ask() returns the text, choose() returns the value picked, and confirm() is true only for a yes. Esc gives null ( false for confirm() ). Questions work in the terminal chat only. Where nobody can answer (the web page, chat platforms, a server) they answer at once with null ( false ) instead of waiting, and agentContext.canAsk() tells you beforehand so a command can say so. Reloading /reload loads the extensions again without leaving the chat: it runs onUnload() of what was loaded, reads ~/.bxagents/bxAgents.yml and the extensions: settings of Agent.yaml anew, and loads what is found, with its commands, keys, status items, prefixes, sources and listeners. An extension that fails to load is reported and left out; the others load. It is for admins and works in the terminal chat only: a served app registers schedulers and ColdBox listeners when it starts, so restart it instead. The web page: slots and web/ Two ways to add to the web page. Both are served with the page; the terminal chat has no page, so they are ignored there. Slots put a string in a named place of the page: header (a chip next to the context size), sidebar (a panel under the list of conversations) or composer (next to the Attach button). The method is called with the agentContext and returns the string: @Slot( "header" ) function badge( agentContext ) { return variables.pings > 0 ? Use the Ping button." } The string is shown as text. Only a slot that says html : true has its string put into the page as markup; that is the author saying it is their own markup, so it must never carry what a visitor typed (use encodeForHTML() ). An empty string shows nothing. The page asks for every slot in one request, GET /api/slots?conversationId= , behind the same sign-in or API key as the rest of the page's API, each time it refreshes the context size. A slot that throws is left out and the reason is put on its extension once. Written as a call: registry.slot( "header", ( agentContext ) => "...", { html : false, name : "badge" } ) . extensions.disable takes extension:method for a slot. web/ is a folder inside a folder extension. # extensions/ An **extension** adds to BxAgents without changing it: chat commands (`/deploy`, `/roll 2d6`), listeners for the events of the chat and of bx-ai, and schedules that run when the agent is served. It is a class that looks and behaves like a ColdBox `ModuleConfig`: it has a `configure()`, an `onLoad()` and an `onUnload()`, its settings come from `Agent.yaml`, and things are handed to it with `$inject`. One file is a whole extension: extensions/ hello.bx /hello roll.bx /roll, /coin standup/ a folder is an extension too Extension.bx commands/Standup.bx schedulers/Reminder.bx A working project with all of these is [`examples/extensions-agent`](https://github.com/ortus-boxlang/bx-agents/tree/development/examples/extensions-agent). ## The smallest extension `extensions/hello.bx`. The file name is the extension's name. class { function configure() { variables.settings = { greeting : "Hello" } } @Command( "hello" ) @Hint( "say hello: /hello " ) function greet( agentContext, commandArguments ) { return agentContext.reply().ok( "#settings.greeting#, #commandArguments#!" ) } } Run `bxAgents chat` and type `/hello Ada`. `/extensions` lists what is loaded. A command method is called with the `agentContext` (the conversation and nothing else; the same object the built-in commands get) and the text after the command name. It returns a `Reply` (`agentContext.reply().ok( "..." )`, `.warn()`, `.keyValues()`, `.grid()`, `.choose()`) or just a string. If it throws, the person sees a warning that names the extension and the chat carries on. ## Annotations Annotations are normal BoxLang annotations on a method. Each one can be written four ways, and every BxAgents annotation takes all four: | Written | Means | Example | |---------|------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------| | bare | defaults; the name comes from the method | `@Command` on `function roll()` is `/roll` | | simple | the main value | `@Command( "deploy" )` | | array | several | `@Alias( [ "dice", "d" ] )` | | struct | every option | `@Command( { name : "deploy", hint : "plan it", admin : true, aliases : [ "ship" ], transports : [ "tui", "web" ] } )` | Shorthand annotations say one option each: `@Hint( "..." )`, `@Admin`, `@Alias( ... )`, `@Transports( [ "tui", "web" ] )`. A struct option wins over a shorthand, and the clash is shown in `/extensions`. Annotation names ignore case. `transports` are where the command runs: `tui` (the terminal chat), `web` (the web page and the HTTP command route) and `gateway` (chat platforms). The default is all three. A chat platform only answers the commands its gateway allows (`gatewaySession.commands.allow`), and a command with `@Admin` only runs for the people listed as admins there. ## Settings The extension says its defaults in `configure()`, as a module does: function configure() { variables.settings = { target : "staging", environments : [ "staging", "production" ] } } The people who use it change them under the extension's name in `Agent.yaml`: ```yaml extensions: deploy: target: production ``` A person can set their own values in `~/.bxagents/bxAgents.yml` (same `extensions:` block); the project's values win over theirs. Nested structs merge key by key, arrays and simple values replace. In the extension, `settings` is the merged struct. ## Lifecycle | Method | When | |---------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------| | `configure()` | once, first. Sets `variables.settings`. No work here | | `onLoad()` | after the settings are merged and everything is injected. Open connections, start timers | | `onUnload()` | when the chat or the server ends. Release them | `this.title`, `this.author`, `this.webURL`, `this.description`, `this.version` and `this.enabled` are read as in a module config, and `this.dependencies = [ "other-extension" ]` loads that extension first. An extension that throws while it loads is shown as failed in `/extensions` with the reason; the others still load. ## Injection Every class of an extension has ``$inject( name, object )`. It puts the object in both the `this` and the `variables` scopes. For private only: `$inject( name, object, "variables" )``. `$read( name )` reads a `variables` entry from outside. BxAgents injects two things before `onLoad()`: `settings` and `log` (`log.info( "..." )`, `.warn()`, `.error()`; what an extension logs is also in `/extensions`). To share an object between the files of an extension, create it in `onLoad()` and `$inject` it where it is needed. The same call is how a test hands an extension a fake. ## A folder extension A folder has the same shape as an agent project: extensions/standup/ Extension.bx optional: the module config (properties, configure(), onLoad(), onUnload()) commands/ one class per command, like the built-in ones schedulers/ BoxLang scheduler classes, started when the agent is served A class in `commands/` extends `models.chat.commands.BaseCommand@bxagents` and says its `name()`, `hint()`, `transports()` and `run( context, args )`. `settings` and `log` are injected into it. ## Schedulers A class in `schedulers/` is a **BoxLang scheduler** : a class with a `configure()` that defines tasks through the `scheduler` property BoxLang gives it, like any other BoxLang scheduler. When the agent is served (`bxAgents serve`, a `.bxa`, a deployed server) it starts in the runtime's scheduler service. Like every class of an extension it is given `settings` (the defaults with the values from `Agent.yaml`) and `log` before `configure()` runs: class { function configure() { scheduler.task( "standup-reminder" ) .call( () => log.info( "Standup time for #settings.channel#" ) ) .everyDayAt( settings.at ) .withNoOverlaps() } } The BoxLang scheduler lifecycle methods (`onStartup()`, `onShutdown()`, `onAnyTaskError()` and the rest) work as usual. Each scheduler is registered as `extension--`, and a scheduler that fails to start is reported on its extension in `/extensions` while the others still run. The terminal chat does not start schedulers: they belong to the served agent. ## Listening to events An extension is also an interceptor. A method named after an event listens to it, exactly like a BoxLang or ColdBox interceptor: class { function onChatInput( data ) { if ( data.text contains "password" ) { data.cancel( "That looks like a password, so it was not sent." ) } } function onAIError( data ) { log.warn( "the model failed" ) } } Two things can be listened to: * **bx-ai events** (`beforeAIAgentRun`, `afterAIModelInvoke`, `onAIError`, `beforeAIToolExecute` and the rest). They fire wherever the agent runs. * **Chat events**, announced by BxAgents: | Event | When | `data` has | A listener can | |-------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------| | `onChatSessionStart` / `onChatSessionEnd` | the terminal chat opens or closes | `agent`, `transport` | | | `onChatInput` | before a message is sent | `text`, `transport` | `cancel( reason )`, or `replace( newText )` | | `onChatTurnStart` / `onChatTurnEnd` | around one turn of the agent | `text`, `transport` (`reply`, `status` at the end) | | | `onChatConversationChange` | `/new`, `/resume`, `/clear`, `/fork` or `/compact` changed the conversation | `line`, `transport` | | | `onChatCommandBefore` | before any command, on every transport | `line`, `name`, `arguments`, `transport` | `cancel( reason )` | | `onChatCommandAfter` | after any command, on every transport | `line`, `name`, `reply`, `transport` | `replace( newReply )` | The session, input, turn and conversation events are the terminal chat's; the two command events fire in the terminal, the web page and on chat platforms alike. A listener that throws is caught: it can never stop a turn, the listeners after it still run, and the error is shown in `/extensions`. `@On` binds a method with another name, or many events at once, and takes the four forms an annotation takes: @On( [ "beforeAIToolExecute", "afterAIToolExecute" ] ) function toolCalled( data ) { log.info( "a tool ran" ) } `@On` naming an event the runtime does not know is reported in `/extensions`, not ignored. ### `interceptors` and `customInterceptionPoints` As in a module config, `configure()` can name classes from the extension's folder to register, each with its own properties, and points of its own to announce: function configure() { variables.interceptors = [ { class : "interceptors.Audit", properties : { level : "info" } } ] variables.customInterceptionPoints = [ "onAuditRecorded" ] } `interceptors/Audit.bx` listens with methods named after events and has `settings`, `log` and `properties` injected. Any extension can then listen to `onAuditRecorded`, and the one that owns it announces it with `BoxAnnounce( "onAuditRecorded", { ... } )`. `extensions.disable` takes `extension:method` to turn one listener off. ColdBox events (`preProcess`, `postProcess` and the rest) are not part of the terminal chat; they fire only in a served agent. ## Keys and status `@Key` binds keys in the terminal chat to a method. On a command method it runs that command, with the same rules and events as typing it; on any other method it calls the method with the `agentContext` and an empty text and shows what it returns. `@Hint` (or `hint` in the struct form) says what it does. ```js @Command @Hint( "count a pulse" ) @Key( "ctrl+g" ) function pulse( agentContext, commandArguments ) { ... } @Key( { keys : [ "ctrl+y", "alt+y" ], hint : "reset the count" } ) function resetPulse( agentContext, commandArguments ) { ... } ``` A key is named `extension:method` (`pulse:pulse`). `/keys` lists it with the built-in ones, and a person can give it other keys under `chat: keys:` in `~/.bxagents/bxAgents.yml`. A key a built-in action already uses, or an earlier extension holds, is refused with a sentence that says so. A typed draft stays in the box while a key runs. Keys are for the terminal chat; the web page and chat platforms have commands. `@Status` is a piece of status next to the size of the context: a method that returns a short text, asked each time the box is drawn in the terminal and after each change to the conversation on the web page (small chips in the header). Return an empty string to show nothing. It must be quick; one that throws is left out and the reason is put on its extension once. ```js @Status function beats( agentContext ) { return variables.beats > 0 ? "beat #variables.beats#" : "" } ``` `extensions.disable` takes `extension:method` for a key or a status item too. ## `register( registry )` What annotations cannot say, because it is worked out in code, is said as calls. If the class has a `register( registry )` method it is called once, right after `configure()`: ```js function register( registry ) { registry.command( "deploy", { run : ( agentContext, commandArguments ) => ..., hint : "ship it", admin : true, aliases : [ "ship" ] } ) registry.key( "ctrl+d", "/deploy", { hint : "ship it" } ) // a key that runs a command line registry.key( "ctrl+o", ( agentContext ) => "opened", { name : "open", hint : "open it" } ) // or any function registry.status( "branch", ( agentContext ) => "main" ) registry.on( "onChatCommandAfter", ( data ) => ... ) // an event, or an array of them } ``` ## Prefixes and `@` sources Both are for the terminal chat only. `@Prefix` claims the start of a line in the message box. The method gets the `agentContext` and the text after the prefix. It answers one of two ways: a `Reply` (or a string) is shown and nothing is sent, and `{ send : "text" }` is sent to the agent as the message, after `onChatInput` has seen it. ```js @Prefix( "%" ) @Hint( "ask for an explanation: % why is the sky blue" ) function explain( agentContext, text ) { return { send : "Explain this in one short paragraph: #text#" } } @Prefix( "=" ) function count( agentContext, text ) { return agentContext.reply().ok( "#text.listToArray( ' ' ).len()# words" ) } ``` `/`, `!`, `#` and `@` are the chat's own, and a lone `?` asks for the keys; a prefix that starts with one of them, is empty or has a space is refused with a sentence. The longest prefix wins. Two extensions on one prefix are a warning and the later layer wins. `@Source( "ticket" )` brings content along with a message the way `@path` brings a file. Write `@ticket:TCK-1` (or `@ticket:"two words"`) and the method is called with the `agentContext` and the query. It returns `{ name, content }`, an array of them or a string; the content goes with the message and the mention stays in it. `@Suggest( "ticket" )` on another method is optional: it returns the values the menu offers as the person types after the colon. It is asked on keystrokes, so it must be quick; one that throws gives no suggestions and the reason is put on its extension once. A source name can be anything that starts with a letter, since files are plain `@path`. ```js @Source( "ticket" ) function ticket( agentContext, query ) { return { name : "ticket #query#", content : tickets[ query ] } } @Suggest( "ticket" ) function ticketNames( agentContext, query ) { return tickets.keyArray() } ``` Written as calls: `registry.prefix( "%", ( agentContext, text ) => ..., { hint : "..." } )` and `registry.source( "ticket", ( agentContext, query ) => ..., { hint : "...", suggest : ( agentContext, query ) => [ ... ] } )`. The person chooses the prefix or the name, by the id `extension:method`, in `~/.bxagents/bxAgents.yml`: ```yaml chat: prefixes: desk:explain: "?%" sources: desk:ticket: issue ``` A choice that cannot be used is reported and the extension's own is kept. `extensions.disable` takes `extension:method` for these too. ## Asking the person A command, key or prefix can put a question to the person while it runs: ```js var title = agentContext.ask( "Title of the ticket?", { default : commandArguments, help : "A short sentence." } ) var priority = agentContext.choose( "Priority?", [ "low", "normal", { value : "high", label : "high", hint : "someone is blocked" } ] ) if ( agentContext.confirm( "Make the #priority# ticket?" ) ) { ... } ``` `ask()` returns the text, `choose()` returns the value picked, and `confirm()` is true only for a yes. Esc gives `null` (`false` for `confirm()`). Questions work in the terminal chat only. Where nobody can answer (the web page, chat platforms, a server) they answer at once with `null` (`false`) instead of waiting, and `agentContext.canAsk()` tells you beforehand so a command can say so. ## Reloading `/reload` loads the extensions again without leaving the chat: it runs `onUnload()` of what was loaded, reads `~/.bxagents/bxAgents.yml` and the `extensions:` settings of `Agent.yaml` anew, and loads what is found, with its commands, keys, status items, prefixes, sources and listeners. An extension that fails to load is reported and left out; the others load. It is for admins and works in the terminal chat only: a served app registers schedulers and ColdBox listeners when it starts, so restart it instead. ## The web page: slots and `web/` Two ways to add to the web page. Both are served with the page; the terminal chat has no page, so they are ignored there. **Slots** put a string in a named place of the page: `header` (a chip next to the context size), `sidebar` (a panel under the list of conversations) or `composer` (next to the Attach button). The method is called with the `agentContext` and returns the string: ```js @Slot( "header" ) function badge( agentContext ) { return variables.pings > 0 ? "#variables.pings# pings" : "" } @Slot( { place : "sidebar", html : true } ) function about( agentContext ) { return "Panel
Use the Ping button." } ``` The string is shown as text. Only a slot that says `html : true` has its string put into the page as markup; that is the author saying it is their own markup, so it must never carry what a visitor typed (use `encodeForHTML()`). An empty string shows nothing. The page asks for every slot in one request, `GET /api/slots?conversationId=`, behind the same sign-in or API key as the rest of the page's API, each time it refreshes the context size. A slot that throws is left out and the reason is put on its extension once. Written as a call: `registry.slot( "header", ( agentContext ) => "...", { html : false, name : "badge" } )`. `extensions.disable` takes `extension:method` for a slot. **`web/`** is a folder inside a folder extension. The build copies it to `/ext//` next to the page, so every file in it (images too) is served from there. The `*.css` and `*.js` files that sit directly in `web/` are linked into the page, in file name order: styles in the head and scripts at the end of the body. An extension turned off by name in `extensions.disable` brings nothing. extensions/panel/ Extension.bx web/ panel.css panel.js logo.png served at /ext/panel/logo.png The page gives scripts one small object, `bxagents`: | | | |----------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------| | `bxagents.slot( place )` | a box of your own in `header`, `sidebar` or `composer`, to draw into | | `bxagents.runCommand( "/ping" )` | runs a slash command as if it were typed | | `bxagents.onRefresh( fn )` | called after each change to the conversation, once the slots are drawn | | `bxagents.refresh()` | asks the page to refresh now | | `bxagents.conversationId()` | the conversation in view | | `bxagents.apiBase` | the page's API path, for your own `fetch` calls | ## Where extensions come from | Layer | Folder | Runs in | |---------|----------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------| | modules | `extensions/` of an installed BoxLang module | everywhere the module is installed | | user | `~/.bxagents/extensions/` | the terminal chat on that machine only | | project | `/extensions/` | the terminal chat, the web page, chat platforms, the server | A later layer wins. An extension with the same name replaces the earlier one, and a command replaces an earlier command of the same name or alias, a built-in included. Both are shown in `/extensions`; nothing is replaced silently. The build copies the project's `extensions/` into the app; a served agent never reads a developer's home folder. ## Turning things off ```yaml extensions: disable: [ roll, "deploy:deploy", "acme-*" ] ``` A plain name turns off the extension of that name (and any command called that); `extension:item` turns off one command; `*` matches any run of characters. Both `Agent.yaml` and `~/.bxagents/bxAgents.yml` accept it. ## Looking at them `/extensions` in the chat, or from the shell: ```bash bxAgents extensions # the list, where each came from and what it added bxAgents extensions --json ``` ## Not yet Extensions cannot yet add gateways, CLI verbs, tools and skills. Those come next.

title: gateways/
body:
gateways/ gateways/*.bx / .json files under this one folder cover two distinct, unrelated things - which kind an entry is depends entirely on whether its configure() struct has an exposes key. Warning Don't confuse these with each other - an HTTP-exposed agent ( exposes: "agent" ) is a REST API for your agent; a channel-adapter gateway ( type: "http" ) is a webhook endpoint for a chat platform or human-in-the-loop approval flow. They generate completely different routes. flowchart TD F["a file under gateways/"] --> Q{"does configure() return
an 'exposes' key?"} Q -->|"yes"| E["EXPOSURE
a route into your agent"] Q -->|"no - it has a 'type' key instead"| C["CHANNEL ADAPTER
a connection to a chat platform"] E --> E1["exposes: agent
route().toAi()"] E --> E2["exposes: mcp
route().toMCP()"] E --> E3["exposes: webui
generated index.html + /api"] C --> C1["mock / cli / http
pull-driven: something calls US"] C --> C2["telegram, slack, discord, email, whatsapp-cloud,
teams, twilio, github, signal
push-style: holds its own connection"] C2 --> S["one GatewaySession
bound to the root agent"] style E fill:#d4edda,stroke:#155724 style C fill:#cce5ff,stroke:#004085 Tip bxAgents add gateway writes this entry for you and the .env stubs it needs, then lists the setup steps that happen outside the project. See add . 1. HTTP/MCP/web-UI exposure ( exposes: "agent" | "mcp" | "webui" ) Exposes the agent, or a local MCP server, over HTTP using ColdBox 8.1's native AI Routing DSL - or a pre-built browser chat UI, documented separately in The web chat UI . Expose the agent: // gateways/expose.bx class { function configure() { return { exposes : "agent", path : "/api/chat" }; } } Generates, in config/Router.bx : route( "/api/chat" ).toAi( "GeneratedAgent" ) which auto-registers four sub-routes: POST /api/chat/invoke , POST /api/chat/stream (SSE), POST /api/chat/batch , GET /api/chat/info . The bare /api/chat path itself is not routable. Expose a local MCP server (see mcp/ ): class { function configure() { return { exposes : "mcp", path : "/mcp/tools", target : "local-server" // must match an mcp/*.bx entry's file name }; } } Generates route( "/mcp/tools" ).toMCP( "local-server" ) . Expose the v1 web chat UI: // gateways/chat.bx class { function configure() { return { exposes : "webui", path : "/chat", apiKeyEnvVar: "CHAT_UI_API_KEY" // optional - see below }; } } Generates a real static /index.html file (served directly - no route needed for it) plus its own dedicated API under a fixed /api prefix, so it never collides with the shell's own files. That API is a generated handlers/ChatUi.bx rather than toAi() , and the entry also brings a generated SQLite store with it. The web UI is a subsystem rather than a single exposure switch - the route list, the store, conversations and preferences, branding and theming, and why it does not use toAi() are all on its own page: The web chat UI . Validation: exposes must be agent , mcp , or webui ; path is required and must be unique across every exposure entry; an mcp exposure's target is required and must match a real mcp/* entry's file name; webui 's apiKeyEnvVar is entirely optional, with no required-field check (see below). A webui entry may list profiles for the page's model picker (see Choosing the model ); each must be declared in Agent.yaml , and no other kind of entry may list them. 2. Channel-adapter gateways ( type: "mock" | "cli" | "http" ) Registers a bx-ai IGateway (a channel adapter for external delivery / human-in-the-loop approval) by name - distinct from exposing the agent's own REST API. // gateways/slack.bx class { function configure() { return { type : "http", secretEnvVar : "SLACK_WEBHOOK_SECRET" }; } } secretEnvVar names an environment variable holding the signing secret - never the secret value itself . Generates, in Application.bx 's onApplicationStart() : aiGatewayRegistry().register( aiGateway( "http", { secret : getSystemSetting( "SLACK_WEBHOOK_SECRET", "" ) } ) ) The secret is resolved live at server startup, matching this project's "secrets stay external" rule everywhere else (see Deployment & Secrets ) - it's never embedded as a literal in generated source, so it's never present in a packaged .bxa either. If the env var is unset, bx-ai's own HttpGateway treats an empty secret as "no signing configured" and rejects requests accordingly, rather than crashing at startup. Validation: type must be mock , cli , or http ; a type: "http" entry requires a secretEnvVar ; the entry's own file/base name must be unique across every channel-adapter entry. mock is test-only; cli is bx-ai's own built-in human-in-the-loop approval channel (a blocking stdin/stdout A/R/Q prompt) - it's what HumanInTheLoopMiddleware attaches by default when no gateway is specified, and is unrelated to BxAgents' own chat verb (which never touches the gateway registry at all). Any channel-adapter entry mounts the bx-ai Gateway surface : one line in config/Router.bx , using ColdBox's own toAiGateway() terminator. route( "/gateways" ).toAiGateway() That single terminator mounts the whole bx-ai Gateway surface: POST /gateways/:gateway/events inbound platform event GET /gateways/:gateway/events the platform's URL verification handshake GET /gateways/interactions/:requestID poll a pending human interaction POST /gateways/interactions/:requestID/decisions submit a human's decision GET /gateways/info what this mount serves This mount is not http -specific. http is one gateway type among many, and the surface is shared: the /interactions routes are the human-in-the-loop approval channel for every gateway, resolved through bx-ai's own gateway registry rather than per-transport. So a project whose only gateway is Telegram, Slack or Discord gets the same /gateways mount - it needs those routes exactly as much, since a paused agent has to be answerable somehow. Warning The routes only reach a running server, so a project relying on human-in-the-loop approval needs serve (or a real deployment), not plain chat . 3. Push-style gateways ( type: "telegram" / "slack" / "discord" / "email" / "whatsapp-cloud" / "teams" / "twilio" / "github" / "signal" , and friends) A different kind of channel adapter from mock / cli / http above: instead of being driven by an inbound HTTP request, a push-style gateway holds its own connection to the platform and pushes inbound messages to your agent as they arrive - the closer-to-"real chat bot" experience. Four transport shapes exist today: Long-poll (Telegram, Email): a scheduled task periodically asks the platform "anything new?" (Telegram's getUpdates , Email's IMAP poll). Persistent websocket (Slack via Socket Mode, Discord via its Gateway API): the gateway holds a live, long-running connection the platform pushes events down in real time. Webhook, pull-driven (WhatsApp Business Cloud API, Microsoft Teams, Twilio SMS, GitHub): the platform calls us over a public HTTP endpoint instead of this gateway holding its own outbound connection - no scheduler task or socket to manage. See their own subsections below. Server-Sent Events (SSE) (Signal, against a locally-run signal-cli daemon): a long-lived, one-way streaming HTTP connection the gateway holds open, reading events as they're pushed down the same response body. See its own subsection below. The nine push-style platforms Each platform gets its own page: its gateways/*.bx config shape, what's required, and (where one exists) the protocol-level detail on how BxAgents talks to it. Telegram Long-poll. botTokenEnvVar only. Slack Persistent websocket, Socket Mode. Discord Persistent websocket, Gateway API, mandatory heartbeats. Email Long-poll IMAP + cbmailservices/bx-mail outbound. WhatsApp Business Cloud Webhook-driven, Meta Graph API. Microsoft Teams Webhook-driven, Bot Framework Activity protocol. Twilio SMS Webhook-driven, form-urlencoded, dual-path TwiML response. GitHub Webhook-driven, @mention -gated issue/PR comment threads. Signal Server-Sent Events, against an external signal-cli daemon. Other types are named back to the person as not read. At most 4 pictures of 5 MB each go with one message, and a picture sent to a profile marked vision: false is refused with that reason, the same checks as the terminal and the web page. Platform What is read Setup Telegram A photo (the largest size within 5 MB) and a document, with the caption as the text None Discord Attachments None Slack Files shared in a message The Slack app needs the files:read scope WhatsApp A picture or document, with its caption None; the media link is fetched with the access token Twilio (MMS) Media sent with the message, even with no text Media links are public unless the account turned on basic auth for media; with that on, they cannot be read Teams, Signal, Email, GitHub Not read Links must be https. the gateway the message came from."] B -->|"yes"| P{"policy"} P -->|"reject"| R["Immediate 'busy' reply.
Nothing is queued - the sender must resend."] P -->|"queue
(the default)"| Q["Enqueue, up to maxQueueDepth.
Runs as its own turn once
the current one finishes."] P -->|"steer"| ST["agent.steerRun( T, text )
Spliced into the SAME run at its next
checkpoint - never a second turn."] P -->|"interrupt"| I["agent.cancelRun( T ), AND enqueue.
The current turn winds down at its next
checkpoint, then this message runs."] Q --> OVER{"queue already at
maxQueueDepth?"} I --> OVER OVER -->|"yes"| R style D fill:#d4edda,stroke:#155724 style R fill:#f8d7da,stroke:#721c24 Warning "Steer" here means Hermes Agent's non-destructive splice - the running turn keeps going and the new text is folded into it. It does not mean what Eve's turnPolicy: "steer" means (cancel the active turn and start a replacement); that behaviour is this vocabulary's interrupt . Info Neither cancelRun() nor steerRun() is instant. Both are signalled and take effect at the run's next checkpoint (before the next LLM call or tool call), so interrupt is "ask the current turn to wind down soon", not "synchronously replace it". # gateways/ `gateways/*.bx`/`.json` files under this one folder cover **two distinct, unrelated things** - which kind an entry is depends entirely on whether its `configure()` struct has an `exposes` key. > **Warning** > > Don't confuse these with each other - an HTTP-exposed agent (`exposes: "agent"`) is a REST API for your agent; a channel-adapter gateway (`type: "http"`) is a webhook endpoint for a chat platform or human-in-the-loop approval flow. They generate completely different routes. ```mermaid flowchart TD F["a file under gateways/"] --> Q{"does configure() return
an 'exposes' key?"} Q -->|"yes"| E["EXPOSURE
a route into your agent"] Q -->|"no - it has a 'type' key instead"| C["CHANNEL ADAPTER
a connection to a chat platform"] E --> E1["exposes: agent
route().toAi()"] E --> E2["exposes: mcp
route().toMCP()"] E --> E3["exposes: webui
generated index.html + /api"] C --> C1["mock / cli / http
pull-driven: something calls US"] C --> C2["telegram, slack, discord, email, whatsapp-cloud,
teams, twilio, github, signal
push-style: holds its own connection"] C2 --> S["one GatewaySession
bound to the root agent"] style E fill:#d4edda,stroke:#155724 style C fill:#cce5ff,stroke:#004085 ``` > **Tip** > > `bxAgents add gateway ` writes this entry for you and the `.env` stubs it needs, then lists the setup steps that happen outside the project. See [`add`](/next/cli-reference/index.html#add-gateway). ## 1. HTTP/MCP/web-UI exposure (`exposes: "agent" | "mcp" | "webui"`) Exposes the agent, or a local MCP server, over HTTP using ColdBox 8.1's native AI Routing DSL - or a pre-built browser chat UI, documented separately in [The web chat UI](/next/conventions/web-ui/index.html). **Expose the agent:** ```javascript // gateways/expose.bx class { function configure() { return { exposes : "agent", path : "/api/chat" }; } } ``` Generates, in `config/Router.bx`: ```javascript route( "/api/chat" ).toAi( "GeneratedAgent" ) ``` which auto-registers **four** sub-routes: `POST /api/chat/invoke`, `POST /api/chat/stream` (SSE), `POST /api/chat/batch`, `GET /api/chat/info`. The bare `/api/chat` path itself is not routable. **Expose a local MCP server** (see [mcp/](/next/conventions/mcp/index.html)): ```javascript class { function configure() { return { exposes : "mcp", path : "/mcp/tools", target : "local-server" // must match an mcp/*.bx entry's file name }; } } ``` Generates `route( "/mcp/tools" ).toMCP( "local-server" )`. **Expose the v1 web chat UI:** ```javascript // gateways/chat.bx class { function configure() { return { exposes : "webui", path : "/chat", apiKeyEnvVar: "CHAT_UI_API_KEY" // optional - see below }; } } ``` Generates a real static `/index.html` file (served directly - no route needed for it) plus its own dedicated API under a fixed `/api` prefix, so it never collides with the shell's own files. That API is a generated `handlers/ChatUi.bx` rather than `toAi()`, and the entry also brings a generated SQLite store with it. The web UI is a subsystem rather than a single exposure switch - the route list, the store, conversations and preferences, branding and theming, and why it does not use `toAi()` are all on its own page: **[The web chat UI](/next/conventions/web-ui/index.html)**. **Validation:** `exposes` must be `agent`, `mcp`, or `webui`; `path` is required and must be unique across every exposure entry; an `mcp` exposure's `target` is required and must match a real `mcp/*` entry's file name; `webui`'s `apiKeyEnvVar` is entirely optional, with no required-field check (see below). A `webui` entry may list `profiles` for the page's model picker (see [Choosing the model](/next/conventions/web-ui/index.html#choosing-the-model)); each must be declared in `Agent.yaml`, and no other kind of entry may list them. ## 2. Channel-adapter gateways (`type: "mock" | "cli" | "http"`) Registers a bx-ai `IGateway` (a channel adapter for external delivery / human-in-the-loop approval) by name - distinct from exposing the agent's own REST API. ```javascript // gateways/slack.bx class { function configure() { return { type : "http", secretEnvVar : "SLACK_WEBHOOK_SECRET" }; } } ``` `secretEnvVar` names an environment variable holding the signing secret - **never the secret value itself** . Generates, in `Application.bx`'s `onApplicationStart()`: ```javascript aiGatewayRegistry().register( aiGateway( "http", { secret : getSystemSetting( "SLACK_WEBHOOK_SECRET", "" ) } ) ) ``` The secret is resolved live at server startup, matching this project's "secrets stay external" rule everywhere else (see [Deployment \& Secrets](/next/deployment-and-secrets/index.html)) - it's never embedded as a literal in generated source, so it's never present in a packaged `.bxa` either. If the env var is unset, bx-ai's own `HttpGateway` treats an empty secret as "no signing configured" and rejects requests accordingly, rather than crashing at startup. **Validation:** `type` must be `mock`, `cli`, or `http`; a `type: "http"` entry requires a `secretEnvVar`; the entry's own file/base name must be unique across every channel-adapter entry. `mock` is test-only; `cli` is bx-ai's own built-in human-in-the-loop **approval** channel (a blocking stdin/stdout A/R/Q prompt) - it's what `HumanInTheLoopMiddleware` attaches by default when no gateway is specified, and is unrelated to BxAgents' own `chat` verb (which never touches the gateway registry at all). **Any channel-adapter entry mounts the bx-ai Gateway surface** : one line in `config/Router.bx`, using ColdBox's own `toAiGateway()` terminator. ```javascript route( "/gateways" ).toAiGateway() ``` That single terminator mounts the whole bx-ai Gateway surface: POST /gateways/:gateway/events inbound platform event GET /gateways/:gateway/events the platform's URL verification handshake GET /gateways/interactions/:requestID poll a pending human interaction POST /gateways/interactions/:requestID/decisions submit a human's decision GET /gateways/info what this mount serves This mount is **not** `http`-specific. `http` is one gateway type among many, and the surface is shared: the `/interactions` routes are the human-in-the-loop approval channel for *every* gateway, resolved through bx-ai's own gateway registry rather than per-transport. So a project whose only gateway is Telegram, Slack or Discord gets the same `/gateways` mount - it needs those routes exactly as much, since a paused agent has to be answerable somehow. > **Warning** > > The routes only reach a running server, so a project relying on human-in-the-loop approval needs [`serve`](/next/cli-reference/index.html#serve) (or a real deployment), not plain `chat`. ## 3. Push-style gateways (`type: "telegram"` / `"slack"` / `"discord"` / `"email"` / `"whatsapp-cloud"` / `"teams"` / `"twilio"` / `"github"` / `"signal"`, and friends) A different kind of channel adapter from `mock`/`cli`/`http` above: instead of being driven by an inbound HTTP request, a push-style gateway holds its own connection to the platform and pushes inbound messages to your agent as they arrive - the closer-to-"real chat bot" experience. Four transport shapes exist today: * **Long-poll** (Telegram, Email): a scheduled task periodically asks the platform "anything new?" (Telegram's `getUpdates`, Email's IMAP poll). * **Persistent websocket** (Slack via Socket Mode, Discord via its Gateway API): the gateway holds a live, long-running connection the platform pushes events down in real time. * **Webhook, pull-driven** (WhatsApp Business Cloud API, Microsoft Teams, Twilio SMS, GitHub): the platform calls **us** over a public HTTP endpoint instead of this gateway holding its own outbound connection - no scheduler task or socket to manage. See their own subsections below. * **Server-Sent Events (SSE)** (Signal, against a locally-run `signal-cli` daemon): a long-lived, one-way streaming HTTP connection the gateway holds open, reading events as they're pushed down the same response body. See its own subsection below. ## The nine push-style platforms Each platform gets its own page: its `gateways/*.bx` config shape, what's required, and (where one exists) the protocol-level detail on how BxAgents talks to it. Control `GatewaySession`'s policy via an optional `gatewaySession` block on the root project's `Agent.yaml`: ```yaml # Agent.yaml gatewaySession: # both optional - these are the defaults policy: queue maxQueueDepth: 50 ``` `policy` must be one of `reject`/`queue`/`steer`/`interrupt` (bx-ai's own `GatewaySession` policy vocabulary, illustrated below) - checked at `build` time so a typo fails loudly instead of surfacing as a runtime error the first time the app boots. > **Warning** > > v1 limitation: exactly one `GatewaySession`, always bound to the project's root agent - matches the existing precedent that `exposes: "agent"` HTTP exposure is also always root-agent-only. A project with subagents cannot yet route different gateways to different subagents. ### Commands in a gateway A message that is one of the session's slash commands is answered by BxAgents itself and never reaches the model, through the same gateway it came in on. Anything else, including a slash word that is not a command here, goes to the agent as before. A choice (a list to pick from) comes back as a numbered list with the command to type for each. By default a safe set is on: `/help`, `/tools`, `/model`, `/info`, `/remember` and `/notes`. They need no conversation of their own and change nothing shared. Narrow it, widen it or switch it off in the same `gatewaySession` block: ```yaml # Agent.yaml gatewaySession: commands: enabled: true # false switches commands off prefix: "/" # one character prefixes: { slack: "!" } # a different one-character prefix for one gateway, by name conversation: false # true also turns on /new, /clear, /compact, /sessions and /resume allow: [ help, info, tools, notes, remember, model ] # the default; any command that runs on a gateway admins: [ "123456789" ] # gateway user ids that may run commands marked for admins ``` Each platform shows the same commands its own way: | Platform | How the commands appear | |---------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------| | Telegram | The bot's `/` menu lists them (`setMyCommands`, sent when the first message arrives). `/info@yourbot` in a group is read as `/info` | | Discord | Registered as application commands when the bot starts, so typing `/` in a server lists them; each takes one optional `args` text. Needs the application id: Discord sends it when the bot connects, or set `applicationId` on the gateway entry. The answer replaces the "thinking" placeholder | | Slack | Slack slash commands are created in the Slack app, not through the API. Define one umbrella command (default `/agent`, option `slashCommand`): `/agent model fast` runs `/model fast` and `/agent` alone runs `/help`. Or define one Slack command per chat command (`/info`). The answer is visible only to the person who typed it. Typed `/word` messages never reach a Slack bot, so use `prefixes` below | | WhatsApp | A "pick one" answer arrives as up to three buttons, or a list for four to ten; a tap runs that command | | Twilio (SMS), Signal and others | A "pick one" answer is a numbered list; reply with just the number. Any other message forgets the list | The prefix can differ per gateway. A Slack workspace has its own `/` commands, so give Slack another character: ```yaml gatewaySession: commands: prefix: "/" prefixes: { slack: "!" } # by gateway name; one character each ``` `build` checks the block: an unknown key, a prefix that is not one character, or an `allow` entry that is not a command that runs on a gateway fails before the app starts. In Telegram a group message such as `/info@yourbot` is read as `/info`. #### Pictures and files A picture or file sent to the bot goes to the agent with the message: pictures as image parts, text files (`.txt`, `.md`, `.json`, `.csv`, code and the like, cut at 100,000 characters) inside the message. Other types are named back to the person as not read. At most 4 pictures of 5 MB each go with one message, and a picture sent to a profile marked `vision: false` is refused with that reason, the same checks as the terminal and the web page. | Platform | What is read | Setup | |------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------| | Telegram | A photo (the largest size within 5 MB) and a document, with the caption as the text | None | | Discord | Attachments | None | | Slack | Files shared in a message | The Slack app needs the `files:read` scope | | WhatsApp | A picture or document, with its caption | None; the media link is fetched with the access token | | Twilio (MMS) | Media sent with the message, even with no text | Media links are public unless the account turned on basic auth for media; with that on, they cannot be read | | Teams, Signal, Email, GitHub | Not read | | Links must be https. A file that cannot be downloaded is named back to the person and the rest of the message goes on. Switch it off with `gatewaySession.attachments: false`. #### Conversation commands `/new`, `/clear`, `/compact`, `/sessions` and `/resume` are off by default, because a chat platform gives every chat one shared conversation: in a group, anyone's `/clear` clears it for everyone. Turn them on with `conversation: true` (or list them in `allow`) when the chats are private or you trust the group. * `/new` moves the chat to a fresh conversation; the old one stays on the list. * `/sessions` lists the conversations the person has had in this app, newest first, and `/resume 2` (or an id) moves the chat back to one. The list is kept in memory, so it lasts until the app restarts; the conversations themselves last as long as the agent's memory does, so an id still works afterwards. * `/clear` and `/compact` act on the conversation the chat is in now. * In a Slack thread, each thread has its own conversation, and `/new` moves only that thread. What each policy actually does with a message that arrives while a turn is still running: ```mermaid flowchart TD M["a message arrives on thread T"] --> B{"is a run already
in flight on T?"} B -->|"no"| D["dispatch a new turn.
The reply streams back through
the gateway the message came from."] B -->|"yes"| P{"policy"} P -->|"reject"| R["Immediate 'busy' reply.
Nothing is queued - the sender must resend."] P -->|"queue
(the default)"| Q["Enqueue, up to maxQueueDepth.
Runs as its own turn once
the current one finishes."] P -->|"steer"| ST["agent.steerRun( T, text )
Spliced into the SAME run at its next
checkpoint - never a second turn."] P -->|"interrupt"| I["agent.cancelRun( T ), AND enqueue.
The current turn winds down at its next
checkpoint, then this message runs."] Q --> OVER{"queue already at
maxQueueDepth?"} I --> OVER OVER -->|"yes"| R style D fill:#d4edda,stroke:#155724 style R fill:#f8d7da,stroke:#721c24 ``` > **Warning** > > "Steer" here means Hermes Agent's non-destructive splice - the running turn keeps going and the new text is folded into it. It does **not** mean what Eve's `turnPolicy: "steer"` means (cancel the active turn and start a replacement); that behaviour is this vocabulary's `interrupt`. > **Info** > > Neither `cancelRun()` nor `steerRun()` is instant. Both are signalled and take effect at the run's **next checkpoint** (before the next LLM call or tool call), so `interrupt` is "ask the current turn to wind down soon", not "synchronously replace it". ### How a push-style gateway stays connected: the shared ColdBox Scheduler Rather than a new background-loop primitive, push-style gateways reach the app's own live ColdBox scheduler singleton (`appScheduler@coldbox` - the same one a hand-written `schedules/Scheduler.bx`, if the project has one, runs under) and register their own named task(s) into it dynamically - a recurring long-poll task for Telegram, for example. **One shared scheduler, every push-style gateway registering its own tasks into it** - never one scheduler per gateway, and never in conflict with a project's own cron jobs. ### Logging Every push-style gateway writes to its own `gateway-` log file (e.g. `gateway-telegram`) via BoxLang's `writeLog()`, rather than one shared/default app log - so an operator can tail exactly the platform they care about without noise from everything else the app logs.

title: gateways/ - Discord
body: Discord Part of the push-style gateways/ family - see there for the shared "secrets stay external" rule, GatewaySession , and the scheduler these gateways run under. This page covers Discord's own config shape and (where BxAgents does anything platform-specific) how it talks to Discord. // gateways/discordChannel.bx class { function configure() { return { type : "discord", botTokenEnvVar: "DISCORD_BOT_TOKEN" // Authorization: Bot <token> on every REST call and inside Identify // intents: 37377 // optional override - defaults to GUILDS+GUILD_MESSAGES+DIRECT_MESSAGES+MESSAGE_CONTENT }; } } Validation: type: "discord" requires botTokenEnvVar . Checked the same way a channel-adapter http entry's secretEnvVar is. Generated registration statement: aiGatewayRegistry().register( aiGateway( "bxModules.bxagents.models.gateways.DiscordGateway", { "botToken" : getSystemSetting( "DISCORD_BOT_TOKEN", "" ) } ) ) Discord's persistent connection - mandatory client-driven heartbeats DiscordGateway connects the same way ( models/gateways/support/DiscordSocketListener.bx , same implements="java:java.net.http.WebSocket$Listener" pattern as Slack), but Discord's Gateway protocol has a requirement Slack's Socket Mode doesn't: the server's own Hello frame (opcode 10) tells the client a heartbeat_interval , and the client must keep sending Heartbeat frames (opcode 1) on that cadence itself or Discord treats the connection as "zombied" and drops it. Since the interval is only known once Hello arrives (not before connecting), the heartbeat is registered as its own scheduler task ( discord-heartbeat-<name> ) dynamically from inside the frame handler, re-registered on every fresh Hello - distinct from every other push-style gateway's fixed-at- registerScheduledTasks() -time task(s), and distinct from Discord's own safety-net watchdog ( discord-watchdog-<name> , every 30s, same role as Slack's). Each heartbeat tick checks whether the previous heartbeat was ever acknowledged ( Heartbeat ACK , opcode 11) - if not, the connection is zombied and gets reconnected proactively rather than left to time out. Reconnects otherwise follow Discord's own documented session model: a Reconnect frame (opcode 7) or most close codes trigger a Resume (opcode 6, replaying the last sequence number) on the new connection when a prior session exists; an Invalid Session frame (opcode 9) with d: false , or a close code Discord documents as session-invalidating ( 4007 , 4009 ), instead forces a fresh Identify (opcode 2). A small, fixed set of close codes ( 4004 bad token, 4010 invalid shard, 4011 sharding required, 4012 invalid API version, 4013 / 4014 invalid/disallowed intents) are non-recoverable per Discord's own docs - the gateway stops rather than retrying a connection that would just fail again. Warning MESSAGE_CONTENT (needed to read message text at all, in both guild channels and DMs) is a Discord privileged Gateway Intent - it must be explicitly enabled for your bot in the Discord Developer Portal, and once your app is verified (100+ guilds), approved by Discord. Without it, every inbound message arrives with an empty content field.
headings: Discord's persistent connection - mandatory client-driven heartbeats

title: gateways/ - Email
body: Email Part of the push-style gateways/ family - see there for the shared "secrets stay external" rule, GatewaySession , and the scheduler these gateways run under. This page covers Email's own config shape and (where BxAgents does anything platform-specific) how it talks to Email. // gateways/emailChannel.bx class { function configure() { return { type : "email", imapHostEnvVar : "IMAP_HOST", imapUsernameEnvVar: "IMAP_USERNAME", imapPasswordEnvVar: "IMAP_PASSWORD", fromAddressEnvVar : "EMAIL_FROM_ADDRESS" // imapPort: 993 // optional override - defaults to 993 (IMAPS) // pollIntervalSeconds: 60 // optional override - defaults to 60 }; } } Validation: type: "email" requires imapHostEnvVar , imapUsernameEnvVar , imapPasswordEnvVar , and fromAddressEnvVar . Checked the same way a channel-adapter http entry's secretEnvVar is. Generated registration statement: aiGatewayRegistry().register( aiGateway( "bxModules.bxagents.models.gateways.EmailGateway", { "imapHost" : getSystemSetting( "IMAP_HOST", "" ), "imapUsername" : getSystemSetting( "IMAP_USERNAME", "" ), "imapPassword" : getSystemSetting( "IMAP_PASSWORD", "" ), "fromAddress" : getSystemSetting( "EMAIL_FROM_ADDRESS", "" ) } ) ) Email - bundled dependencies, and degraded threading/HITL EmailGateway is the only push-style gateway that doesn't speak its platform's API directly. Outbound mail goes through ColdBox's own cbmailservices module ( MailService@cbmailservices , its BXMail protocol - which itself just calls BoxLang's own bx:mail component, from the bx-mail module) rather than a hand-rolled HTTP/SMTP call. Both ship inside BxAgents : bx-mail as a bundled BoxLang module and cbmailservices in the ColdBox runtime that build copies into the app, so there is nothing to install. EmailGateway resolves MailService@cbmailservices manually off application.cbController.getWireBox() (see ScheduledGatewayBase.resolveScheduler() 's own docblock for why - this class is constructed directly by aiGateway() , entirely outside WireBox, so inject="" is never honored on it), the same way the scheduler itself is resolved. Because neither bx-mail nor cbmailservices receive mail (only send it), inbound is hand-rolled IMAP via the JDK-standard jakarta.mail API - confirmed reachable on this project's own classpath transitively ( bx-mail depends on commons-email2-jakarta , which itself depends on jakarta.mail-api + an Angus Mail implementation), verified empirically this session against the real jars, not assumed. A scheduled task ( email-poll-<name> ) polls IMAP for unseen mail, same shape as Telegram's long-poll. Threading and human-in-the-loop are both degraded relative to the chat-platform gateways, and getDeclaredCapabilities() deliberately omits "interactiveActions" to say so honestly: Threading uses real Message-ID / In-Reply-To / References headers for an ORDINARY reply (the gateway always knows the inbound Message-ID it's replying to, so setting In-Reply-To on the outbound reply is reliable) - a v1 simplification threads on References ' first entry (else In-Reply-To , else the message's own Message-ID ), not a full walk of the chain. Human-in-the-loop has no native button/component surface at all - requestHumanInteraction() sends a plain-text email listing the allowed decision keywords and asks the human to reply with one as the first line. Correlating that reply back to the right pending request can't rely on In-Reply-To the way ordinary replies do (cbmailservices' send() doesn't expose what Message-ID the outbound approval email itself got assigned), so it's done via a [bxagents:<requestID>] tag embedded in the Subject line instead - the same technique real email-based support-ticket systems use for the identical reason. A reply's first line is matched against the request's own allowed decisions (exact or prefix, case-insensitive); an unrecognized reply is passed through verbatim rather than re-prompted, left for bx-ai's own HITL coordinator to reject.

# GitHub

Part of the push-style [gateways/](/next/conventions/gateways/index.html) family - see there for the shared "secrets stay external" rule, `GatewaySession`, and the scheduler these gateways run under. This page covers GitHub's own config shape and (where BxAgents does anything platform-specific) how it talks to GitHub.

```javascript
// gateways/githubChannel.bx
class {
	function configure() {
		return {
			type               : "github",
			tokenEnvVar        : "GITHUB_TOKEN",           // a personal access token (repo/issues+PR read+write scope)
			webhookSecretEnvVar: "GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET",  // HMAC key verifying X-Hub-Signature-256 on inbound webhooks
			botNameEnvVar      : "GITHUB_BOT_NAME"         // the bot's own GitHub login - matched as "@botName" in comments
			// apiBaseUrl: "https://api.github.com"   // optional override - defaults to "https://api.github.com"
		};
	}
}
```

**Validation:** `type: "github"` requires `tokenEnvVar`, `webhookSecretEnvVar`, and `botNameEnvVar`. Checked the same way a channel-adapter `http` entry's `secretEnvVar` is.

Generated registration statement:

```javascript
aiGatewayRegistry().register( aiGateway( "bxModules.bxagents.models.gateways.GitHubGateway", { "token" : getSystemSetting( "GITHUB_TOKEN", "" ), "webhookSecret" : getSystemSetting( "GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET", "" ), "botName" : getSystemSetting( "GITHUB_BOT_NAME", "" ) } ) )
```

## GitHub - `@mention`-gated issue/PR comment threads

`GitHubGateway` treats each issue, PR, or inline review-comment thread as a chat conversation - the agent responds when explicitly `@mentioned` in a comment, and replies by posting a new comment back to the same thread. Webhook-driven the same way every other gateway in this section is:

```javascript
post( "/webhooks/github" ).toHandler( "GitHub.process" )
```

Ported from Vercel Eve's real GitHub channel (`packages/eve/src/public/channels/github/`, MIT licensed) - `X-Hub-Signature-256` verification is confirmed the **identical construction** to WhatsApp Cloud's own Meta scheme (HMAC-SHA256 over the raw body, hex, `sha256=` prefix) - the only webhook gateway in this project that reuses another one's exact signature algorithm, rather than needing its own. Only `issue_comment` and `pull_request_review_comment` events with `action: "created"` get dispatched (matching Eve's own only-default-handled event kinds - `issues`/`pull_request`/`check_suite`/`check_run`/`workflow_run` have no default dispatch in Eve either, and aren't wired here); every other event kind is acknowledged (200) but ignored, to avoid GitHub's retry/disable-hook-on-failure behavior for events this gateway doesn't act on.

**The dispatch gate is a genuine `@mention` requirement** , ported from Eve's own `extractGitHubCommentTrigger()`: a comment only reaches the agent if it contains `@<botName>` followed by end-of-string or a non-identifier character (so a bot named `mybot` never fires on a comment mentioning `@mybot2`) - confirmed via a real regex-lookahead smoke test this session before trusting it. The matched `@mention` token is stripped from the text before it reaches the agent. Bot-loop prevention mirrors Eve's own three-part guard: any comment whose author has GitHub's own `type: "Bot"`, whose login matches `{botName}[bot]`, or whose body contains this gateway's own `<!-- bxagents:posted -->` marker (appended to every comment it posts) is ignored outright, even if it happens to contain a mention.

A "conversation" is identified by one of two shapes, matching Eve's own model: `repo:{owner}/{repo}:issue:{issueNumber}` for an ordinary issue/PR comment thread, or `repo:{owner}/{repo}:review-comment:{reviewThreadRootCommentId}` for an inline PR review-comment thread - replies to a review thread always go to the **thread root** comment (`comment.in_reply_to_id ?? comment.id`), not the specific comment being replied to, so a multi-message back-and-forth stays one thread. Outbound replies POST to `repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues/{issueNumber}/comments` (ordinary threads) or `repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/{pullRequestNumber}/comments/{reviewCommentId}/replies` (review threads).
> **Info**
>
> v1 auth is a plain personal access token (`tokenEnvVar`), not Eve's own GitHub App JWT + installation-token flow - simpler and more directly portable for a first cut (Eve itself supports a pre-resolved-token bypass for exactly this reason, which is what this maps onto). A future GitHub App mode is a natural extension, not built here. Unlike Eve (which has no delivery-id dedup at all, confirmed absent by reading its source), `GitHubGateway` dedups by `X-GitHub-Delivery` via a bounded FIFO cache, matching WhatsApp Cloud's own `wamid` dedup discipline.
> **Warning**
>
> No repo checkout/code-editing (Eve's own `checkout.ts`, which clones the repo into a sandbox so the agent can read/edit code) was ported - this is a comment-in/comment-out chat surface only. Human-in-the-loop is degraded the same way Twilio's is (no native button/card affordance) - `requestHumanInteraction()` posts a comment asking the human to `@mention` the bot again in a reply with one of the allowed decisions, correlated by conversationID (not a per-request tag), the same v1 simplification Twilio's own HITL fallback uses.

title: gateways/ - Microsoft Teams
body: Microsoft Teams Part of the push-style gateways/ family - see there for the shared "secrets stay external" rule, GatewaySession , and the scheduler these gateways run under. This page covers Microsoft Teams's own config shape and (where BxAgents does anything platform-specific) how it talks to Microsoft Teams. // gateways/teamsChannel.bx class { function configure() { return { type : "teams", appIdEnvVar : "TEAMS_APP_ID", // the bot's own Microsoft App ID (also the inbound JWT's required aud claim) appPasswordEnvVar : "TEAMS_APP_PASSWORD" // OAuth2 client-credentials secret // tenantId: "..." // optional override for single-tenant apps - defaults to "botframework.com" (multi-tenant) }; } } Validation: type: "teams" requires appIdEnvVar and appPasswordEnvVar . Checked the same way a channel-adapter http entry's secretEnvVar is. Generated registration statement: aiGatewayRegistry().register( aiGateway( "bxModules.bxagents.models.gateways.TeamsGateway", { "appId" : getSystemSetting( "TEAMS_APP_ID", "" ), "appPassword" : getSystemSetting( "TEAMS_APP_PASSWORD", "" ) } ) ) Microsoft Teams - Bot Framework Activity protocol TeamsGateway is webhook-driven the same way WhatsAppCloudGateway is - it extends BaseGateway directly, and Microsoft's own Bot Connector service calls us , over a single generated route: post( "/webhooks/teams" ).toHandler( "Teams.process" ) Unlike WhatsApp Cloud there's no GET verify handshake (Bot Framework has no equivalent of Meta's hub.challenge ) - every inbound activity arrives as a signed POST, verified via a bearer JWT in the Authorization header rather than an HMAC signature over the body. The JWT is checked against Bot Connector's own JWKS ( https://login.botframework.com/v1/.well-known/openidconfiguration → its jwks_uri ) - RS256 signature, aud must equal the bot's own configured appId , iss must equal Bot Connector's fixed issuer string ( https://api.botframework.com ), both with a 5-minute clock-skew allowance. This is genuine RSA/JWT verification built from BoxLang's own Java interop ( java.security.Signature , java.security.KeyFactory , java.math.BigInteger ) - no external JWT library. Outbound calls use a separate OAuth2 client-credentials token (fetched from login.microsoftonline.com/{tenantId}/oauth2/v2.0/token , cached and refetched 60s before its stated expiry). Ported from Vercel Eve's real Teams channel ( packages/eve/src/public/channels/teams/ , MIT licensed) - the OAuth2 flow, the JWT verification scheme, the v3/conversations/{id}/activities[/{activityId}] REST triad, and the Adaptive Card human-in-the-loop shape (schema 1.5, one Action.Submit button per allowed decision) all mirror that implementation. Hermes Agent's own msgraph_webhook.py is unrelated despite the similar "Microsoft webhook" naming - it implements Microsoft Graph change-notification webhooks (mailbox/drive/list resource-change events, a different Microsoft product surface with no working outbound Teams messaging at all) and nothing from it was ported here. Warning v1 scope is personal (1:1 DM) conversations only - group chat and channel-wide messages need bot-mention gating and a different reply-threading model that Eve itself implements but this port doesn't, matching every other push-style gateway's own DM-first v1 scoping. A message chunk limit of 4000 chars is used (Eve's own Adaptive Card text-truncation constant) rather than the Bot Framework protocol's true 80 KiB ceiling, for UI readability. Info The Bot Connector JWKS is fetched once and cached for the gateway instance's lifetime - if Microsoft ever rotates its signing keys without a matching kid already cached, verification would start failing until the gateway (and thus the whole app) restarts. No periodic cache invalidation is built for v1. The JWT verification logic itself was empirically verified this session against a real, locally-generated RSA keypair and hand-signed test JWTs (valid signature accepted, tampered signature/wrong audience/expired token all rejected with 401) - not just read against Eve's source.

# Microsoft Teams

Part of the push-style [gateways/](/next/conventions/gateways/index.html) family - see there for the shared "secrets stay external" rule, `GatewaySession`, and the scheduler these gateways run under. This page covers Microsoft Teams's own config shape and (where BxAgents does anything platform-specific) how it talks to Microsoft Teams.

```javascript
// gateways/teamsChannel.bx
class {
	function configure() {
		return {
			type                : "teams",
			appIdEnvVar         : "TEAMS_APP_ID",         // the bot's own Microsoft App ID (also the inbound JWT's required aud claim)
			appPasswordEnvVar   : "TEAMS_APP_PASSWORD"    // OAuth2 client-credentials secret
			// tenantId: "..."   // optional override for single-tenant apps - defaults to "botframework.com" (multi-tenant)
		};
	}

```

Generated registration statement:

