markdown:
# The Agent Definition - Agent.yaml

`Agent.yaml` is the **only required file** in a BxAgents project (beside the
instructions it points at). It is plain settings - a name, a model, and any optional
extras - and the build turns it into a real
[BX AI agent](https://ai.ortusbooks.com/main-components/agents/class-based-agents).
No code needed.

```yaml
name: my-agent
description: A helpful assistant
model: openai/gpt-5
instructions: |
  You are a helpful assistant.
```

That is a complete agent. `bxAgents new` scaffolds this shape for you (see
[Lesson 4](/next/course/04-scaffolding-your-first-agent/index.html)), with the system prompt in an
`instructions.md` beside it (see [Lesson 6](/next/course/06-instructions-and-system-prompt/index.html)).
> **Info**
>
> A folder holds **one** agent definition. An `Agent.yaml` together with an
> `Agent.bx` (or an `Agent.yml`) in the same folder is an error, and the build names
> both files so you can keep one.

## The keys

|                 Key                  |                                                            What it does                                                            |
|--------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `name`                               | The agent's name. Also its WireBox binding key, so it must be unique across the whole project.                                     |
| `model`                              | A `provider/model` slug (see below).                                                                                               |
| `description`                        | Optional.                                                                                                                          |
| `instructions`                       | Inline system prompt. An `instructions.md` beside the file wins when both exist.                                                   |
| `tools`                              | Module tools this agent gets, as `item@module` or `*@module` (see [Lesson 9](/next/course/09-giving-your-agent-tools/index.html)). |
| `toolOptions`                        | Options for a module's tools, keyed by module name.                                                                                |
| `subAgents`                          | Names of sibling folders under `subagents/` (see [Lesson 11](/next/course/11-composing-subagents/index.html)).                     |
| `mcpServers`                         | Remote MCP servers the agent can call (see [Lesson 17](/next/course/17-hosting-mcp-servers/index.html)).                           |
| `security`, `memory`, `checkpointer` | Guardrails, conversation memory and human-in-the-loop state.                                                                       |
| `gatewaySession`                     | How chat gateways queue sessions (see [Lesson 14](/next/course/14-connecting-chat-platforms/index.html)).                          |
| `agentApi`                           | The always-on agent route.                                                                                                         |
| `environments`                       | Per-environment overrides (see below).                                                                                             |

An **unknown key is an error** that lists the valid ones, so a typo such as `modle:`
can never quietly do nothing. Wrong types and empty values are errors too.
> **Info**
>
> The checkpointer is the one thing the build fills in unasked. An agent reachable
> from a gateway with no checkpointer has silently broken human-in-the-loop, so a
> definition that sets none still gets the `cache` default.

## The model slug

`model` is BxAgents' own convention - bx-ai itself takes `provider` and `model` as two
separate arguments. BxAgents splits the slug **on the first `/` only**:

|          `model` value          |   provider   |        model         |
|---------------------------------|--------------|----------------------|
| `openai/gpt-5`                  | `openai`     | `gpt-5`              |
| `openrouter/anthropic/claude-x` | `openrouter` | `anthropic/claude-x` |
| `mock/mock-model`               | `mock`       | `mock-model`         |

`mock` is a real provider that never makes a network call - useful for tests (see
[Lesson 19](/next/course/19-testing-your-agent/index.html)) and for following this course with no API key
at all.

## Adding settings

Other settings are just more keys:

```yaml
name: with-mcp-servers-agent
model: openai/gpt-5
mcpServers:
  - https://example.com/mcp
```

## Environment overrides

`environments` maps an environment name (`production`, `development`, or any custom
name) to a block of overrides:

```yaml
name: my-agent
model: openai/gpt-5

environments:
  production:
    model: openai/gpt-5-mini
  test:
    model: mock/mock-model
```

The active environment resolves, highest wins: `--environment` CLI flag \>
`BX_AGENTS_ENV` env var \> `"development"` default. `bxAgents build --environment=production`
picks it up. Only the active block is applied, on top of the top-level keys. You'll use
this exact mechanism for the `mock` provider in your tests ([Lesson 19](/next/course/19-testing-your-agent/index.html)),
which is why `bxAgents new` already gives you a `test` block.

Full reference: [Agent.yaml](/next/conventions/agent-yaml/index.html).

## When you need code: Agent.bx

`Agent.yaml` covers almost every agent. Reach for the advanced class form, `Agent.bx`,
only when the definition itself needs code: hooks, dynamic instructions, tools
registered in code, an overridden method, or computing the environment with
`detectEnvironment()`. It is a real class extending bx-ai's `AiAgent`, which the build
instantiates:

```javascript
class extends="bxModules.bxai.models.runnables.AiAgent" {

	function init() {
		super.init(
			name        : "my-agent",
			description : "A helpful assistant",
			instructions: "You are a helpful assistant.",
			model       : aiModel( provider: "openai", params: { model: "gpt-5" } )
		)
		return this
	}

}
```

Scaffold one with `bxAgents new --class`, or start in YAML and switch later: create the
`Agent.bx`, move the settings across, and delete the `Agent.yaml`. Full reference:
[Agent.bx](/next/conventions/agent-bx/index.html).

Next: [Lesson 6 - instructions.md and the System Prompt](/next/course/06-instructions-and-system-prompt/index.html)

title: Lesson 6: instructions.md and the System Prompt
body: instructions.md and the System Prompt instructions.md is optional - bxAgents new scaffolds a starter one for you to edit, but you have two equally valid choices for where your agent's system prompt lives: Set instructions inline in Agent.yaml . Drop an instructions.md file beside Agent.yaml and let the build wire it in. Letting the file win If instructions.md exists, the build emits: withInstructions( fileRead( "instructions.md" ) ) which wins over an inline instructions in Agent.yaml (or whatever a class set). This is the more common pattern in practice - it keeps the prompt as plain text you can edit without touching BoxLang code, and it's easy to diff in a pull request. # instructions.md You are a helpful assistant for a small hardware store. Be concise. If a customer asks about a product you don't have information on, say so rather than guessing. Setting it inline instead name: my-agent model: openai/gpt-5 instructions: | You are a helpful assistant. Keep answers short. Do this for a short prompt, or when you'd rather keep everything about the agent in one file. If both exist, instructions.md wins; if neither exists, the build fails and says so. A prompt that must be generated or templated in code belongs in the advanced class-based Agent.bx (see the end of Lesson 5 ). Which one should you pick? Start with instructions.md - it's what bxAgents new scaffolds, it's the simplest mental model ("the system prompt is this file"), and it plays nicely with the rest of this course, which assumes plain-text prompts throughout. Reach for the inline instructions key only for a short prompt, and for code only once you have a concrete reason to (templating, environment-specific prompts assembled from smaller pieces, etc.). Try it Open the instructions.md that Lesson 4 's bxAgents new created and write a real system prompt for whatever kind of agent you want to build in this course - a support bot, a code reviewer, anything. You'll build and run it in the next two lessons. Next: Lesson 7 - Building Your Agent
markdown:
# instructions.md and the System Prompt

`instructions.md` is **optional** - `bxAgents new` scaffolds a starter one for you to
edit, but you have two equally valid choices for where your agent's system prompt
lives:

1. Set `instructions` inline in `Agent.yaml`.
2. Drop an `instructions.md` file beside `Agent.yaml` and let the build wire it in.

## Letting the file win

If `instructions.md` exists, the build emits:

```javascript
withInstructions( fileRead( "instructions.md" ) )
```

which wins over an inline `instructions` in `Agent.yaml` (or whatever a class set).
This is the more common pattern in
practice - it keeps the prompt as plain text you can edit without touching BoxLang
code, and it's easy to diff in a pull request.

```markdown
# instructions.md
You are a helpful assistant for a small hardware store. Be concise. If a customer
asks about a product you don't have information on, say so rather than guessing.
```

## Setting it inline instead

```yaml
name: my-agent
model: openai/gpt-5
instructions: |
  You are a helpful assistant.
  Keep answers short.
```

Do this for a short prompt, or when you'd rather keep everything about the agent in one
file. If both exist, `instructions.md` wins; if neither exists, the build fails and says
so. A prompt that must be generated or templated in code belongs in the advanced
class-based `Agent.bx` (see the end of [Lesson 5](/next/course/05-agent-bx/index.html)).

## Which one should you pick?

Start with `instructions.md` - it's what `bxAgents new` scaffolds, it's the simplest
mental model ("the system prompt is this file"), and it plays nicely with the rest of
this course, which assumes plain-text prompts throughout. Reach for the inline
`instructions` key only for a short prompt, and for code only once you have a concrete
reason to (templating, environment-specific prompts assembled from smaller pieces,
etc.).

## Try it

Open the `instructions.md` that [Lesson 4](/next/course/04-scaffolding-your-first-agent/index.html)'s
`bxAgents new` created and write a real system prompt for whatever kind of agent you
want to build in this course - a support bot, a code reviewer, anything. You'll build
and run it in the next two lessons.

Next: [Lesson 7 - Building Your Agent](/next/course/07-building-your-agent/index.html)

.build/app is never written"] C -->|"clean"| D["4 · Generate"] D --> E["5 · Normalize + write manifest"] E --> F[".build/manifest.json

This is the entire point of paying the assembly cost once, at build time, instead of deferring it into every request. ## Useful flag: `--verbose` ```bash bxAgents build --verbose ``` Prints one line per build phase live as it runs - what got resolved/discovered/ validated, per-phase counts, which agents ended up registered in `config/WireBox.bx` and under which names, whether a scheduler was found, and a final timing line. Silent otherwise, so it costs nothing when you don't need it. ## Try it ```bash cd my-agent bxAgents build --verbose ``` You should see a `.build/app/` directory appear, and a manifest describing exactly what went into it. # Talking to Your Agent

Once you've built your project ([Lesson 7](/next/course/07-building-your-agent/index.html)), there are
three ways to run it - all load the exact same `GeneratedAgentFactory.bx` and build
the exact same agent tree, so they never diverge from each other.

## `chat` - an interactive REPL

```bash
bxAgents chat                                  # fast, in-process
bxAgents chat --server [--port=<port>]         # full app, own throwaway server
bxAgents chat --connect=http://127.0.0.1:8080  # full app, server you already run
```

Uses BoxLang's own `MiniConsole` for line reading. Requires a real interactive
terminal (it shells out to `stty` for raw mode - it won't work piped or
non-interactively). Type `exit` or `quit` to leave.

The default mode loads the generated factory directly in this process - fastest, but
without anything ColdBox brings (no scheduler, no interceptors, no
gateway registry). When that matters, `--server` boots a real miniserver and drives the
REPL over HTTP against your project's always-on agent route, and `--connect` does the
same against a server you already have running. Both HTTP modes **stream** the reply
token by token and carry the server's `threadId` across turns, so a session is one
conversation rather than a series of unrelated first messages.

## `invoke` - one non-interactive turn

```bash
bxAgents invoke --message="What's the weather in Boston?" [--json]
```

Exists for scripting and CI, where `chat`'s TTY requirement is a hard blocker. By
default this loads the generated factory in-process, the same path `chat` uses
internally, just without the REPL loop - no `serve` prerequisite at all. `--json`
prints `{"response": "..."}` instead of plain text.

Add `--server` to instead launch a real, throwaway `boxlang-miniserver` process and
send the message as a genuine HTTP request to your project's always-on agent route -
no `gateways/` entry needed (those come in [Lesson 13](/next/course/13-exposing-http-and-mcp/index.html)). Like
`serve`, it needs `boxlang-miniserver` on `PATH`.

## `serve` - a real HTTP server

```bash
bxAgents serve --port=8080
```

Requires a prior `build` and requires `boxlang-miniserver` on `PATH` (see
[Lesson 3](/next/course/03-installing-bxagents/index.html)). Launches a real server process pointed at
`.build/app`, scoped to its own `.build/runtime` BoxLang home so each project's
compiled-class cache stays isolated.
> **Warning**
>
> The **very first** request to a freshly booted app's `toAi()` route can
> transiently fail - a genuine ColdBox/WireBox lazy-injection race, not a BxAgents
> bug. It succeeds reliably after that. Send a warm-up request before relying on a
> freshly deployed route under load.

## Testing without a real API key

Every one of these needs a real model to talk to a real provider - but you don't need
one yet. Add a `test` environment override to `Agent.yaml` (covered fully in
[Lesson 19](/next/course/19-testing-your-agent/index.html)):

```yaml
environments:
  test:
    model: mock/mock-model
```

then `bxAgents build --environment=test && bxAgents chat` runs entirely against bx-ai's
built-in mock provider - no network call, no API key.

## Try it

```bash
export OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-...   # or use the mock override above
bxAgents chat
```

Say hello to the agent you scaffolded and wrote instructions for in
[Lessons 4-6](/next/course/04-scaffolding-your-first-agent/index.html). It's a real, running agent - you
just haven't given it anything to *do* yet. That starts next lesson.

Full reference: [Quick Start](/next/getting-started/quick-start/index.html), [CLI Reference](/next/cli-reference/index.html).

Next: [Lesson 9 - Giving Your Agent Tools](/next/course/09-giving-your-agent-tools/index.html)

markdown:
# Giving Your Agent Tools

Any `.bx` file under `tools/` (searched recursively, so `tools/nested/Search.bx` works
too) that declares an `@AITool`-annotated function becomes a callable tool for your
agent.

```javascript
// tools/Greeter.bx
class {

	@AITool( "Say hello to someone by name." )
	function sayHello( name ) {
		return "Hello, " & arguments.name & "!";
	}

}
```

BxAgents doesn't scan or interpret `@AITool` annotations itself at build time - it
just discovers one entry per `.bx` file (for name-collision checking) and copies the
whole `tools/` folder **verbatim** into the generated app. At startup, the generated
app calls bx-ai's own scanner (`aiToolRegistry().scan( "tools" )`), which does the real
reflection work. This statement is only emitted at all if your project actually has a
`tools/` folder with files in it.

## Whose tools are they?

An agent gets its own `tools/` folder and nothing else: a root agent's tools are not
given to its subagents, and the other way round. Tools that *modules* register with
bx-ai (its built-ins, `bx-playwright`, ...) are only attached when the agent asks for
them in `Agent.yaml`:

```yaml
tools:
  - now@bxai
  - "*@bxplaywright"
```

See [Agent.yaml](/next/conventions/agent-yaml/index.html#tools) for the details.

## Naming

The discovered entry name is the file's own base name - `Greeter.bx` becomes
`Greeter`. Two tool files with the same base name, even in different subfolders (since
discovery is flat by base name), fail validation with a duplicate-name error.

## What's excluded

Dotfiles are ignored by discovery, and `.env`/dotfiles inside `tools/` are never
copied into the build output even if present.

## Rebuilds are clean

`tools/` is copied with a wipe-then-write strategy on every `build` - a file you
delete from your project's `tools/` folder never lingers as stale output from a
previous build.

## Try it

Add a real tool to the agent you've been building:

```javascript
// tools/GetTime.bx
class {

	@AITool( "Get the current server time." )
	function now() {
		return dateTimeFormat( now(), "yyyy-mm-dd HH:nn:ss" );
	}

}
```

Rebuild and chat with it:

```bash
bxAgents build
bxAgents chat
> What time is it?
```

Full reference: [tools/](/next/conventions/tools/index.html).

Next: [Lesson 10 - Packaging Skills](/next/course/10-packaging-skills/index.html)

title: mcp/
body:
mcp/ MCP (Model Context Protocol) works two directions - consuming remote servers, and hosting your own. flowchart LR subgraph consume["CONSUMING - declared on Agent.yaml via mcpServers"] direction LR AG["your agent"] -->|"calls out at runtime"| RM["a remote MCP server
https://example.com/mcp"] end subgraph host["HOSTING - one file per server under mcp/"] direction LR TL["tools/
your @AITool functions"] -->|"a named SUBSET"| MS["mcpServer( 'localServer' )
registered at onApplicationStart()"] MS --> GW["a gateways/ entry with exposes: mcp
route( '/mcp/tools' ).toMCP()"] GW -->|"reachable over HTTP"| OC["some outside MCP client"] end style consume fill:#e7f1ff,stroke:#004085 style host fill:#eaf6ec,stroke:#155724 Nothing links the two: an agent consuming remote servers need not host one, and a hosted server is reachable only if a gateways/ entry exposes it. Tip bxAgents add mcp client github adds a server to Agent.yaml with its credential as an environment placeholder, and bxAgents add mcp server writes the mcp/ file and the gateways/ entry that serves it. See add . Consuming remote servers Declared directly on Agent.yaml (not a file under mcp/ ), via mcpServers : # Agent.yaml name: my-agent model: openai/gpt-5 mcpServers: - https://example.com/mcp - url: https://other.com/mcp name: other Each entry is either a bare URL string or a mapping. A mapping can carry the credentials the server wants: mcpServers: - name: github url: https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/ token: ${env.GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN} - url: https://other.com/mcp headers: X-Api-Key: ${env.OTHER_API_KEY} timeout: 20000 Key Meaning url Required. The server's address name A label for the file. It is not sent to the server token A bearer token. Must be an ${env.NAME} placeholder: a token written in the file is a build error password , user Basic authentication. password must be an ${env.NAME} placeholder headers Extra request headers. Values can use ${env.NAME} timeout Milliseconds allowedHosts The host names the server's address may have, for example [api.example.com, "*.example.com"] . *.example.com matches any subdomain, not example.com itself. A request to any other host is refused before anything is sent redirects false treats a redirect answer as a failure and never follows it maxResponseBytes Refuses an answer longer than this many characters handshake true sends the MCP initialize handshake before the first call prefix Tools are named prefix__tool , so two servers cannot clash toolFilter A list of tool names; only these are given to the agent Placeholders are replaced with the environment variable when the app starts , never at build time, so a secret stays out of the project and out of a packaged .bxa . A variable that is not set fails the agent at startup and names it; one that is set but empty lets the agent start, the server refuses the connection, and bx-ai logs that and carries on without that server's tools. Any other key is a build error that lists the valid ones. The entries are passed into the generated aiAgent(mcpServers: [...]) call. No network connection is ever attempted at build time - reachability is a runtime concern; an unreachable server at build time is not a build error. This section is for servers reached over the web; servers that run as a program on the agent's machine are next. bxAgents new offers GitHub, Stripe, Notion, Atlassian, Cloudflare, Supabase and Git and writes the entry and the .env stub for you. Subagents can declare their own mcpServers independently - each node in the agent tree gets its own resolved list. Servers that run as a program An entry with command starts an MCP server as a program on the machine that runs the agent, and talks to it over the program's standard input and output: mcpServers: - name: git command: [uvx, mcp-server-git] prefix: git toolFilter: [git_status, git_diff, git_log] - name: browser command: [bxplaywright, mcp] env: PLAYWRIGHT_API_KEY: ${env.PLAYWRIGHT_API_KEY} cwd: . Key Meaning command Required. A list: the program, then its arguments. It is never run through a shell name A label for the file env Environment variables for the program. A variable whose name contains KEY , TOKEN , SECRET , PASSWORD or CREDENTIAL must be an ${env.NAME} placeholder cwd The folder the program starts in inheritEnv false starts it with only env . Default true maxRestarts How many times in a row a program that died is started again. Default 2 timeout Milliseconds per request prefix , toolFilter As for web servers The program starts on the first call and is closed when the app stops. command cannot be combined with url , and the keys that only make sense for a web server ( token , headers , user , password , allowedHosts , redirects , maxResponseBytes , handshake ) are a build error on it. When the app starts, the programs your agents declare become bx-ai's mcp.stdio.allowedCommands setting, so the process starts only what the project declared. A list you set yourself (for example in .boxlang.json ) is left alone and must name the programs. bxAgents doctor warns when a program is not on the PATH. A program runs with your user's rights on the machine that hosts the agent. Read what you start, and use toolFilter to limit what the agent may call. Hosting a local server Each mcp/*.bx file is a local MCP server your project hosts, exposing a subset of your tools/ as MCP tools: // mcp/localServer.bx class { function configure() { return { description : "Internal tools MCP server", version : "1.0.0", cors : "*", // optional - CORS origin(s) allowed to call this server; omit for none tools : [ "sayHello" ] // names of tools already declared under tools/ }; } } The entry's discovered name is its filename ( localServer.bx → localServer ), not any name field inside its own configure() struct - a project may still set one for documentation, but it's ignored for naming/registration purposes. cors is optional and defaults to an empty string (no CORS header) when omitted - passed straight through as mcpServer() 's 4th positional argument. At build time, the file is copied verbatim into the generated app's mcp/ folder, and a registration statement is emitted into Application.bx 's onApplicationStart() : mcpServer( "localServer", "Internal tools MCP server", "1.0.0", "*" ) .registerTool( aiToolRegistry().get( "sayHello" ) ) mcpServer(name, ...) is a global, name-keyed singleton getter in bx-ai - registering it once at startup is all that's needed; there's no WireBox mapping involved (unlike the agent-exposure singleton used by toAi() ). Exposing a local server over HTTP A local mcp/* server isn't reachable over HTTP on its own - pair it with a gateways/ exposure entry naming it as the target : // gateways/expose-mcp.bx class { function configure() { return { exposes : "mcp", path : "/mcp/tools", target : "localServer" }; } } Validation An mcpServers entry (struct form) needs a url or a command , not both and not neither. An mcpServers entry that's neither a non-empty string nor a struct fails validation. A command must be a list of non-empty words. A key for the other kind of server, an env secret written in the file, and a mistyped allowedHosts , redirects , handshake , prefix or toolFilter fail validation. A gateways/ entry with exposes: "mcp" and a target that doesn't match any discovered mcp/* entry fails validation.

This section is for servers reached over the web; servers that run as a program on the agent's machine are next. [`bxAgents new`](/next/guides/new-wizard/index.html#mcp-servers) offers GitHub, Stripe, Notion, Atlassian, Cloudflare, Supabase and Git and writes the entry and the `.env` stub for you. Subagents can declare their own `mcpServers` independently - each node in the agent tree gets its own resolved list. ### Servers that run as a program An entry with `command` starts an MCP server as a program on the machine that runs the agent, and talks to it over the program's standard input and output: ```yaml mcpServers: - name: git command: [uvx, mcp-server-git] prefix: git toolFilter: [git_status, git_diff, git_log] - name: browser command: [bxplaywright, mcp] env: PLAYWRIGHT_API_KEY: ${env.PLAYWRIGHT_API_KEY} cwd: . ``` | Key | Meaning | |------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------| | `command` | Required. A list: the program, then its arguments. It is never run through a shell | | `name` | A label for the file | | `env` | Environment variables for the program. A variable whose name contains `KEY`, `TOKEN`, `SECRET`, `PASSWORD` or `CREDENTIAL` must be an `${env.NAME}` placeholder | | `cwd` | The folder the program starts in | | `inheritEnv` | `false` starts it with only `env`. Default `true` | | `maxRestarts` | How many times in a row a program that died is started again. Default 2 | | `timeout` | Milliseconds per request | | `prefix`, `toolFilter` | As for web servers | The program starts on the first call and is closed when the app stops. `command` cannot be combined with `url`, and the keys that only make sense for a web server (`token`, `headers`, `user`, `password`, `allowedHosts`, `redirects`, `maxResponseBytes`, `handshake`) are a build error on it. When the app starts, the programs your agents declare become bx-ai's `mcp.stdio.allowedCommands` setting, so the process starts only what the project declared. A list you set yourself (for example in `.boxlang.json`) is left alone and must name the programs. [`bxAgents doctor`](/next/cli-reference/index.html) warns when a program is not on the PATH. A program runs with your user's rights on the machine that hosts the agent. Read what you start, and use `toolFilter` to limit what the agent may call. ## Hosting a local server Each `mcp/*.bx` file is a local MCP server your project hosts, exposing a subset of your `tools/` as MCP tools: ```javascript // mcp/localServer.bx class { function configure() { return { description : "Internal tools MCP server", version : "1.0.0", cors : "*", // optional - CORS origin(s) allowed to call this server; omit for none tools : [ "sayHello" ] // names of tools already declared under tools/ }; } } ``` The entry's discovered name is its **filename** (`localServer.bx` → `localServer`), not any `name` field inside its own `configure()` struct - a project may still set one for documentation, but it's ignored for naming/registration purposes. `cors` is optional and defaults to an empty string (no CORS header) when omitted - passed straight through as `mcpServer()`'s 4th positional argument. At build time, the file is copied verbatim into the generated app's `mcp/` folder, and a registration statement is emitted into `Application.bx`'s `onApplicationStart()`: ```javascript mcpServer( "localServer", "Internal tools MCP server", "1.0.0", "*" ) .registerTool( aiToolRegistry().get( "sayHello" ) ) ``` `mcpServer(name, ...)` is a global, name-keyed singleton getter in bx-ai - registering it once at startup is all that's needed; there's no WireBox mapping involved (unlike the agent-exposure singleton used by `toAi()`). ## Exposing a local server over HTTP A local `mcp/*` server isn't reachable over HTTP on its own - pair it with a [`gateways/`](/next/conventions/gateways/index.html) exposure entry naming it as the `target`: ```javascript // gateways/expose-mcp.bx class { function configure() { return { exposes : "mcp", path : "/mcp/tools", target : "localServer" }; } } ``` ## Validation * An `mcpServers` entry (struct form) needs a `url` or a `command`, not both and not neither. * An `mcpServers` entry that's neither a non-empty string nor a struct fails validation. * A `command` must be a list of non-empty words. A key for the other kind of server, an `env` secret written in the file, and a mistyped `allowedHosts`, `redirects`, `handshake`, `prefix` or `toolFilter` fail validation. * A `gateways/` entry with `exposes: "mcp"` and a `target` that doesn't match any discovered `mcp/*` entry fails validation.

# Models and profiles

Which model an agent uses is written in `Agent.yaml`. The build maps it onto bx-ai's settings, so you never write a `boxlang.json` for it. The names are bx-ai's own: `provider`, `model`, `params`, `options`, `providers`, `profiles`.

```yaml
provider: openai                 # the default model
model: gpt-5
params: { temperature: 0.2 }

providers:                       # settings for another provider
  claude: { params: { max_tokens: 4000 }, options: { timeout: 90 } }

profiles:                        # named combinations
  fast:    { description: Cheap and quick, provider: openai, model: gpt-5-mini, params: { temperature: 0 } }
  planner: { description: Careful planning, provider: claude, model: claude-opus-4, apiKeyEnv: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }
defaultProfile: fast             # optional

embeddings:    { provider: openai, model: text-embedding-3-small }
speech:        { provider: openai, model: tts-1, voice: nova }
transcription: { provider: openai, model: whisper-1 }
image:         { provider: openai, model: gpt-image-1, size: 1024x1024 }
```

## The default model

`provider`, `model` and `params` are the model every agent uses when it says nothing else. `model: openai/gpt-5` still works as shorthand for `provider: openai` plus `model: gpt-5`. `params` are request parameters such as `temperature` and `max_tokens`. `options` (timeout and similar) apply to the default provider.

`contextWindow` and `vision` say what the default model can do, see [What the project knows about a model](#what-the-project-knows-about-a-model).

## Other providers

`providers` holds `params` and `options` for a provider by name, for the ones you use through a profile or a subagent. `bxAgents add provider` writes one for you. The key for each provider is read from its usual environment variable (`OPENAI_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, ...); `bxAgents doctor` tells you when one is missing.

## Profiles

A profile is a named combination: a provider, a model, params, options and the name of the environment variable that holds its key. It can carry a `description`.

|            Key            |                                                              Meaning                                                               |
|---------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `description`             | For people and the terminal and web pickers.                                                                                       |
| `provider`, `model`       | What it runs on. A profile without a provider uses the default provider.                                                           |
| `params`, `options`       | Layered on top of the provider's and the default's: `params` from the default, then the provider, then the profile.                |
| `apiKeyEnv`               | The **name** of the variable that holds the key. A key itself is never written in `Agent.yaml`; a profile that has one is refused. |
| `contextWindow`, `vision` | What the project knows about the model, see below.                                                                                 |

A profile cannot be named `default` or like a provider (`openai`, `claude`, ...), because both are selected by name. `defaultProfile` picks which profile is used when nothing asks for another one: it is the default model. If the file also has a top-level `model`, the profile wins and the build and `doctor` warn that the `model` line is ignored. Without a `defaultProfile`, the top-level `provider` and `model` are the default. `bxAgents add profile` writes a profile (and `--default` the `defaultProfile`) without touching the rest of the file; see [`add profile`](/next/cli-reference/index.html#add-profile).

## What the project knows about a model

bx-ai has no way to ask a model how much it can hold or whether it can see images, so you can say so, on the default model and on each profile:

```yaml
contextWindow: 128000      # tokens the default model can hold
vision: true               # the default model can see images
profiles:
  fast:
    provider: openai
    model: gpt-5-mini
    contextWindow: 400000
    vision: false
```

`contextWindow` is a whole number of tokens and `vision` is `true` or `false`; `build` refuses anything else. Both are optional and nothing is guessed: a model with no entry is simply unknown. bx-ai does not read them. The chat shows them in `/info` and `/model`, and uses `contextWindow` for the share of the window the context takes (`/context`, the status bar and the web header). Later, `vision` decides whether an image may be pasted.

## Testing a model

`/ping` in the chat and `bxAgents models test` send a model one tiny question through bx-ai and say whether it answered, and how long it took, so a wrong key or model name shows up before a conversation does. See [`models`](/next/cli-reference/index.html#models) and [Models in the chat](/next/cli-reference/index.html#models-in-the-chat).

## Which agent uses what

An agent uses its own `profile:`, else its own `model:` (a `provider/model` slug), else the default. Every subagent inherits the root's settings, and may set its own `model` or `profile`:

```yaml
# subagents/planner/Agent.yaml
name: planner
profile: planner
```

`providers`, `profiles`, `defaultProfile`, `params` and the capability keys apply to the whole app, so they belong in the project's own `Agent.yaml`; a subagent that sets them fails validation.

## Capability defaults

`embeddings`, `speech`, `transcription` and `image` set bx-ai's defaults for `aiEmbed()`, `aiSpeak()`, `aiTranscribe()` and `aiImage()`. They do not take profiles. bx-ai has one audio provider, so `speech` and `transcription` must name the same one. `bxAgents add capability` writes one; see [`add capability`](/next/cli-reference/index.html#add-capability).

## Validation and tests

`bxAgents build` checks all of the above by bx-ai's own rules and names the file and the key. Under `bxAgents test` every profile runs on the `mock` provider, so a test never reaches the network.

## How it reaches bx-ai

The build writes the settings to `config/bxai-settings.json` in the app, and the app merges them into bx-ai's settings when it starts, before ColdBox boots and builds the agents. They travel with the app wherever it runs (`serve`, a `.bxa`, a container).

title: modules/
body: modules/ modules/ holds BoxLang module dependencies your agent needs - one immediate subfolder per module, discovered by folder name (not recursive - only the top level of modules/ is enumerated). modules/ └── my-extra-module/ ├── module.json └── ... Declaring dependencies between modules A module folder may include a module.json with a dependsOn array naming other modules/* entries by folder name: { "dependsOn": [ "some-other-module" ] } This is BxAgents' own dependency-declaration convention for validation purposes - it is independent of BoxLang's own module-loading mechanism. Info Today build validates modules/ and records each entry (with a content hash) in the manifest , but it does not copy the folders into the generated app or load them. To give the generated app a library, use the project lib/ folder described in Installation . Validation A module.json that isn't valid JSON fails the build with a parse error naming the offending module. A dependsOn entry naming a module that isn't itself a discovered modules/* folder fails validation ("depends on unknown module"). Circular dependencies are rejected the same way subagent cycles are - full cycle path reported, DFS-based detection, no code generation happens until the graph is acyclic. A module.json is entirely optional - a module folder with none is assumed to have no declared dependencies.
markdown:
# modules/

`modules/` holds BoxLang module dependencies your agent needs - one immediate subfolder per module, discovered by folder name (not recursive - only the top level of `modules/` is enumerated).

    modules/
    └── my-extra-module/
        ├── module.json
        └── ...

## Declaring dependencies between modules

A module folder may include a `module.json` with a `dependsOn` array naming other `modules/*` entries by folder name:

```json
{
	"dependsOn": [ "some-other-module" ]
}
```

This is BxAgents' own dependency-declaration convention for validation purposes - it is independent of BoxLang's own module-loading mechanism.
> **Info**
>
> Today `build` validates `modules/` and records each entry (with a content hash) in the [manifest](/next/manifest/index.html), but it does not copy the folders into the generated app or load them. To give the generated app a library, use the project `lib/` folder described in [Installation](/next/getting-started/installation/index.html#adding-your-own-libraries).

## Validation

* A `module.json` that isn't valid JSON fails the build with a parse error naming the offending module.
* A `dependsOn` entry naming a module that isn't itself a discovered `modules/*` folder fails validation ("depends on unknown module").
* **Circular dependencies** are rejected the same way [subagent](/next/conventions/subagents/index.html) cycles are - full cycle path reported, DFS-based detection, no code generation happens until the graph is acyclic.
* A `module.json` is entirely optional - a module folder with none is assumed to have no declared dependencies.

# Quick Start

![A terminal session: bxAgents new scaffolds a project, bxAgents build assembles a ColdBox app, bxAgents inspect prints the agent, model and environment, and bxAgents serve starts it on http://127.0.0.1:8080](/next/assets/cli-quickstart.svg)

This walks through the full lifecycle of a BxAgents project: scaffold, edit, build, run.

## 1. Scaffold a project

```bash
bxAgents new my-agent
```

At a terminal this asks what the agent should do (its model, tools, MCP servers, channels, how people reach it, where it deploys) and writes the project to match; see [the new wizard](/next/guides/new-wizard/index.html). To skip the questions, pass a model:

```bash
bxAgents new my-agent --model=openai/gpt-5
```

`--model` is a `provider/model` slug - see [the model slug](/next/conventions/agent-bx/index.html#the-model-slug) for how it's parsed. `--name` and `--description` are optional; `--name` defaults to the target directory's own name.

This creates:

    my-agent/
    ├── Agent.yaml
    ├── instructions.md
    ├── tools/
    ├── skills/
    ├── subagents/
    ├── gateways/
    ├── schedules/
    ├── mcp/
    ├── interceptors/
    ├── modules/
    └── tests/
        ├── box.json
        └── specs/
            └── AgentSpec.bx

Plus a `.env` (with `BOXLANG_HOME=.build/runtime`; put your provider API keys there too) and a `.gitignore`. BoxLang loads the `.env` from the project root itself.

This is the `minimal` starter - the default when `--template` is omitted. `new` can also scaffold one of 7 other built-in starters (`--template=webui-chat|slack-bot|telegram-bot|github-bot|mcp-server|scheduled|multi-agent`), each adding a bit of pre-wired content (a gateway, a scheduler) on top of the same skeleton, or skip scaffolding entirely and create the project from an existing GitHub repo (`--repo=owner/repo`) or a ForgeBox package (`--forgebox=<slug>`) instead - see the [CLI Reference](/next/cli-reference/index.html#new) for the full list and how each one works. The agent is defined by an `Agent.yaml` by default; pass `--class` to scaffold the advanced, class-based `Agent.bx` instead (see [Agent.bx](/next/conventions/agent-bx/index.html)).

`Agent.yaml` looks like this (`--description` adds a `description:` line):

```yaml
# Your agent. Most agents need nothing more than this file and instructions.md.
# For code in the definition (hooks, dynamic instructions), scaffold with --class.
name: my-agent
model: openai/gpt-5

environments:
  # `bxAgents test` builds against this override by default (see
  # BaseAgentSpec.bx) so a fresh project's tests need no API key or
  # network access - swap the model to test against a real provider.
  test:
    model: mock/mock-model
```

The agent is just this file plus `instructions.md`. See [Agent.yaml](/next/conventions/agent-yaml/index.html) for every key.

Every convention folder is created empty - add files to the ones your agent actually needs and delete (or just ignore) the rest.

## 2. Edit

Open `instructions.md` and write the agent's system prompt, and adjust `name`, `description` or `model` in `Agent.yaml` as you like. Add a tool:

```javascript
// tools/Greeter.bx
class {

	@AITool( "Say hello to someone by name." )
	function sayHello( name ) {
		return "Hello, " & arguments.name & "!";
	}

}
```

See the [Conventions](/next/conventions/agent-yaml/index.html) section for every other folder (`skills/`, `subagents/`, `gateways/`, `schedules/`, `mcp/`, `interceptors/`, `modules/`).

## 3. Test it

```bash
box install        # once, to fetch testbox into lib/testbox (`new` already tried this for you)
bxAgents test
```

The scaffolded `tests/specs/AgentSpec.bx` passes out of the box - it builds your agent against the `mock` provider (no API key or network needed) and asserts on a scripted response. See [tests/](/next/conventions/testing/index.html) for `mockResponses()` and the custom matchers (`toHaveCalledTool`, etc.) available to your own specs.

## 4. Build

```bash
bxAgents build
```

Runs the full [build pipeline](/next/build-pipeline/index.html) - config resolution, discovery, validation, code generation, manifest normalization - and writes a real ColdBox application to `.build/app/`, plus `.build/manifest.json`. Run `bxAgents build --environment=production` to build against an `Agent.yaml` environment override (see [Agent.yaml](/next/conventions/agent-yaml/index.html#environments)).

If your project fails validation (duplicate tool names, an unknown model provider, a gateway entry with a bad path, ...) `build` fails with every collected error - not just the first one.

## 5. Run it

Two ways to talk to the built agent - both load the exact same `GeneratedAgentFactory.bx` and build the exact same agent tree, so they never diverge:

**Interactively, from the terminal:**

```bash
bxAgents chat
```

**Over HTTP** , via a real [`boxlang-miniserver`](https://boxlang.ortusbooks.com/getting-started/running-boxlang/miniserver) process:

```bash
bxAgents serve --port=8080
```

If your project has a `gateways/*` entry with `{ exposes: "agent", path: "/api/chat" }`, the agent is now reachable at `POST http://localhost:8080/api/chat/invoke` (and `/stream`, `/batch`, `/info` - see [gateways/](/next/conventions/gateways/index.html)).
> **Warning**
>
> The very first request to a freshly booted app's `toAi()` route can transiently fail. Send a warm-up request before relying on it under load.

## 6. Inspect, package, deploy

```bash
bxAgents inspect              # how the agent is composed: agents, tools, env vars, checks
bxAgents package --version=1.0.0   # writes dist/my-agent-1.0.0.bxa + .sha256
bxAgents deploy --destination=/path/to/somewhere   # copies the newest .bxa there
```

See [The Manifest](/next/manifest/index.html) and [Deployment \& Secrets](/next/deployment-and-secrets/index.html).

## 7. Clean up

```bash
bxAgents clean
```

Removes `.build/` and `dist/` only - your source conventions (`Agent.yaml`, `tools/`, etc.) are never touched.

## Next steps

* Walk through every convention folder in [Conventions](/next/conventions/agent-yaml/index.html).
* Look at the working sample projects in [`examples/`](https://github.com/ortus-boxlang/bx-agents/tree/development/examples).
* See every verb's flags in [CLI Reference](/next/cli-reference/index.html).

markdown:
# schedules/

`schedules/Scheduler.bx` - if present - is a **real, hand-written ColdBox scheduler class** , passed through into the build untouched (a plain file copy to `config/Scheduler.bx`, no generation, no translation):

```javascript
// schedules/Scheduler.bx
class extends="coldbox.system.web.tasks.ColdBoxScheduler" {

	function configure() {
		task( "nightly" )
			.call( () => getInstance( "SupportBot" ).run( "cleanup" ) )
			.everyDayAt( "00:00" )
			.withNoOverlaps()
	}

}
```

There's nothing BxAgents-specific about the body of that file - it's ColdBox's own scheduler DSL, in full: `.every( 15, "minutes" )`, `.everyDayAt( "09:00" )`, `.onWeekdays( "08:30" )`, `.everyWeekOn()`, `.startOn()`/`.endOn()`/`.between()`, `.when()`, `.withNoOverlaps()`, `before()`/`after()`/`onSuccess()`/`onFailure()` hooks, timezones - anything ColdBox's `ScheduledTask` supports, this project doesn't limit or reinterpret. (An earlier version of this convention was a `{ cron, action }` data shape translated into ColdBox's frequency-method DSL here - that translation only covered a narrow subset of cron and threw away everything else the real scheduler API offers, so it's gone. If you're migrating an old project, see below.)
> **Tip**
>
> `bxAgents add schedule` adds a task for you: say when it runs and what to tell the agent. See [`add`](/next/cli-reference/index.html#add-schedule).

## Retrieving an agent

Every agent in the project's tree - the root project's own agent definition and every `subagents/*` entry, however deeply nested - is registered in the generated `config/WireBox.bx` under its own declared `name` (the `name` in its `Agent.yaml`, or, for a class-based `Agent.bx`, the one set via `super.init()` or a `configure()`-declared `name` overriding it). A schedule reaches whichever agent it wants with a plain `getInstance( "TheAgentName" )` - no BxAgents-specific lookup, just WireBox, exactly like the `getInstance()` calls elsewhere in a ColdBox app.

```yaml
# subagents/researcher/Agent.yaml
name: ResearchBot
description: Researches a topic
model: openai/gpt-5
```

```javascript
// schedules/Scheduler.bx
task( "weekly-digest" )
	.call( () => getInstance( "ResearchBot" ).run( "summarize this week's findings" ) )
	.everyWeekOn( 1, "08:00" )
```

Because `name` is now also a WireBox binding key, it must be **unique across the whole project** - `build` fails validation if two agents (root or subagent, at any depth) share a name, including two that both leave it unset and silently default to `"BxAi"`. See [subagents/](/next/conventions/subagents/index.html#retrieving-an-agent-from-schedulesschedulerbx) for the distinction between a subagent's folder name (used to wire `subAgents: [...]`) and its own declared `name` (used here).

## Validation

* `build` only ever looks for exactly one file: `schedules/Scheduler.bx`. Anything else in `schedules/` (including old `{ cron, action }` files from before this convention changed) is ignored - `build` emits a warning if `schedules/` exists but has no `Scheduler.bx`, so a schedule that quietly stopped running is at least visible.
* Beyond that, `schedules/Scheduler.bx` is real code - the same kind of "we can't meaningfully validate this without a real ColdBox boot" territory as any other BoxLang class. A syntax error or a bad `getInstance()` name surfaces when the generated app actually boots (`serve`), not at `build` validation time.

## Migrating from the old `{ cron, action }` convention

Before, each file under `schedules/` was its own `{ cron: "0 0 * * *", action: "cleanup" }` entry, translated into a ColdBox frequency-method call against the single root `"GeneratedAgent"` binding. To migrate: delete those files, add one `schedules/Scheduler.bx` extending `coldbox.system.web.tasks.ColdBoxScheduler`, and for each old entry add a `task( name ).call( () => getInstance( "TheAgentName" ).run( "action text" ) )` with whichever real ColdBox frequency method or `.cron()` call matches the old cron expression.

markdown:
# skills/

Each immediate subfolder of `skills/` that contains a `SKILL.md` file is one skill, following the Claude Agent Skills convention: YAML frontmatter (`name`, `description`) followed by a body of freeform instructions.

    skills/
    └── greeting/
        └── SKILL.md

```markdown
---
name: greeting
description: How to greet people warmly.
---

Always greet the user warmly and use their name if known.
```

> **Tip**
>
> `bxAgents add skill <name>` creates `skills/<name>/SKILL.md` with the frontmatter and a body to fill in. See [`add`](/next/cli-reference/index.html#add-skill).

## Naming

The skill's name is its frontmatter `name:` if present; otherwise it falls back to the folder name (`greeting/` with no frontmatter name would be discovered as `greeting` anyway, but an explicit `name:` always wins even if it differs from the folder). Two skills resolving to the same name fail validation with a duplicate-name error.

A folder without a `SKILL.md` inside it is not discovered as a skill at all - it's simply ignored (useful for scratch subfolders, assets kept alongside a skill under a different structure, etc., as long as they don't sit directly under `skills/` themselves without a `SKILL.md`).

## Skills from the registry

Skills from skills.boxlang.io are installed with `bxAgents skills install <owner/repo/skill>`, not copied by hand. They go in `.agents/skills/` (bx-ai's own default folder), out of source control; `.agents/skills.lock.json` is committed and `build` restores from it. Both folders go into the build, and a skill in `skills/` with the same name wins. See [`skills`](/next/cli-reference/index.html#skills).

## How it's wired at runtime

`skills/` is copied verbatim into the generated app (same wipe-then-write, dotfile-excluding copy as [`tools/`](/next/conventions/tools/index.html)). The generated `config/ColdBox.bx` always points bx-ai's own `skillsDirectory` module setting at `/skills`:

```javascript
moduleSettings = {
	bxai : { skillsDirectory : "/skills" }
}
```

> **Info**
>
> bx-ai's own default `skillsDirectory` is `/.agents/skills` - a different path than BxAgents' `skills/` convention. The generator always overrides it explicitly so the app's `skills/` folder is the one bx-ai actually loads from. Skills installed under your project's `.agents/skills/` are copied into it at build time; you never need to set this yourself.

title: subagents/
body:
subagents/ subagents/ holds nested agents, each an ordinary BxAgents project of its own - an Agent.yaml + instructions.md (and optionally its own tools/ , skills/ , etc.). A subagent's tools/ belong to it alone, and its tools: list is its own; neither is inherited from or shared with its parent: my-agent/ ├── Agent.yaml # subAgents: [ researcher ] ├── instructions.md └── subagents/ └── researcher/ ├── Agent.yaml └── instructions.md A subagent is wired to its parent by name, declared in the parent's Agent.yaml subAgents list - the subagents/ FOLDER name to wire at build time: # Agent.yaml name: my-agent model: openai/gpt-5 subAgents: - researcher The same list in a class-based Agent.bx (the advanced form ) goes in configure() , distinct from super.init() 's own subAgents argument (which takes already-built AiAgent instances, not names). A project can mix the two forms: a YAML root with a class subagent, or the reverse. At build time, bx-ai's addSubAgent() wraps each built subagent instance as a callable tool on the parent automatically - there's no separate tool-wrapping step to write yourself. Tip bxAgents add subagent creates the folder, asks the same questions as new for its model and tools, and adds it to the parent's subAgents . --parent= nests it under another subagent. See add . Flat namespace, sibling references Every subagent - no matter how deeply another subagent's own config references it - lives directly under the root project's subagents/ folder. A subagent's own declared subAgents names reference sibling entries in that same root-level folder, not a folder nested under itself. This keeps the discovery/validation model simple: one flat directed graph over subagents/ 's immediate subfolders, rather than a tree that could nest arbitrarily deep on disk. Flat on disk, a graph in config, built bottom-up - the three views of the same project: flowchart LR subgraph disk["ON DISK - always flat, one level under the ROOT project"] direction TB R1["subagents/A/"] R2["subagents/B/"] R3["subagents/C/"] end subgraph declared["DECLARED - each definition's own subAgents list"] direction TB GA["A"] --> GB["B"] --> GC["C"] end subgraph built["BUILT - leaf-first, in GeneratedAgentFactory.bx"] direction TB O1["1. build C"] --> O2["2. build B
with the built C"] --> O3["3. build A
with the built B"] end disk -.->|"names resolve
against siblings"| declared declared -.->|"a parent needs its
children already built"| built style disk fill:#eef2f7,stroke:#5a6570 style declared fill:#e7f1ff,stroke:#004085 style built fill:#eaf6ec,stroke:#155724 A cycle in the declared graph ( A -> B -> A ) is rejected at validation, before any of this is generated; a diamond (two parents sharing one descendant) is fine. Build order Subagents are built leaf-first (bottom-up): if A declares subAgents: ["B"] and B declares subAgents: ["C"] , the generated GeneratedAgentFactory.bx builds C , then B (passing in the built C instance), then A (passing in the built B instance) - never the other way around, since a parent's aiAgent() call needs its children's already-built instances. Validation A subagent name in subAgents that doesn't correspond to a real subagents/{name}/ folder (holding an Agent.yaml or Agent.bx ) fails validation with a clear "references unknown subagent [...]" error - this applies to every node's subAgents list, including the root project's own definition, not just nested subagents. Circular references ( A → B → A ) are rejected at validation time, with the full cycle path reported (e.g. A -> B -> A ), before any code generation happens. A "diamond" shape - two subagents both depending on the same shared descendant - is not a cycle and builds fine; only genuine cycles are rejected. A missing Agent.yaml / Agent.bx inside a discovered subagents/* folder is reported as its own validation error, and so is a folder holding both ( BxAgents.AmbiguousAgentDefinition ) - a folder holds one definition. Every node's own DECLARED name (root + every subagent's own definition) must be unique across the whole project - see below. Retrieving an agent from schedules/Scheduler.bx Two different names are in play, and they're not interchangeable: The folder name under subagents/ ( researcher above) is what subAgents: [ "..." ] references - it's purely a build-time wiring concern. The subagent's own declared name (its agent definition's name field, e.g. "ResearchBot" ) is what you retrieve it by at runtime - every agent in the tree (root + every subagent) is registered in config/WireBox.bx under this name, so schedules/Scheduler.bx (or any other WireBox-aware code) reaches it with a plain getInstance( "ResearchBot" ) . These two names can differ, and often will - the folder name is an implementation detail, the declared name is the one that matters everywhere else (prompts, WireBox retrieval). Because it's now also a WireBox binding key, build fails validation if two agents in the tree - however deeply nested - end up with the same declared name , including two that both leave it unset and silently share the "BxAi" default.

# subagents/ `subagents/` holds nested agents, each an ordinary BxAgents project of its own - an `Agent.yaml` + `instructions.md` (and optionally its own `tools/`, `skills/`, etc.). A subagent's `tools/` belong to it alone, and its `tools:` list is its own; neither is inherited from or shared with its parent: my-agent/ ├── Agent.yaml # subAgents: [ researcher ] ├── instructions.md └── subagents/ └── researcher/ ├── Agent.yaml └── instructions.md A subagent is wired to its parent by name, declared in the parent's `Agent.yaml` `subAgents` list - the `subagents/` FOLDER name to wire at build time: ```yaml # Agent.yaml name: my-agent model: openai/gpt-5 subAgents: - researcher ``` The same list in a class-based `Agent.bx` (the [advanced form](/next/conventions/agent-bx/index.html)) goes in `configure()`, distinct from `super.init()`'s own `subAgents` argument (which takes already-built `AiAgent` instances, not names). A project can mix the two forms: a YAML root with a class subagent, or the reverse. At build time, bx-ai's `addSubAgent()` wraps each built subagent instance as a callable tool on the parent automatically - there's no separate tool-wrapping step to write yourself. > **Tip** > > `bxAgents add subagent ` creates the folder, asks the same questions as `new` for its model and tools, and adds it to the parent's `subAgents`. `--parent=` nests it under another subagent. See [`add`](/next/cli-reference/index.html#add-subagent). ## Flat namespace, sibling references Every subagent - no matter how deeply another subagent's own config references it - lives directly under the **root** project's `subagents/` folder. A subagent's own declared `subAgents` names reference **sibling** entries in that same root-level folder, not a folder nested under itself. This keeps the discovery/validation model simple: one flat directed graph over `subagents/`'s immediate subfolders, rather than a tree that could nest arbitrarily deep on disk. Flat on disk, a graph in config, built bottom-up - the three views of the same project: ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph disk["ON DISK - always flat, one level under the ROOT project"] direction TB R1["subagents/A/"] R2["subagents/B/"] R3["subagents/C/"] end subgraph declared["DECLARED - each definition's own subAgents list"] direction TB GA["A"] --> GB["B"] --> GC["C"] end subgraph built["BUILT - leaf-first, in GeneratedAgentFactory.bx"] direction TB O1["1. build C"] --> O2["2. build B
with the built C"] --> O3["3. build A
with the built B"] end disk -.->|"names resolve
against siblings"| declared declared -.->|"a parent needs its
children already built"| built style disk fill:#eef2f7,stroke:#5a6570 style declared fill:#e7f1ff,stroke:#004085 style built fill:#eaf6ec,stroke:#155724 ``` A cycle in the declared graph (`A -> B -> A`) is rejected at validation, before any of this is generated; a diamond (two parents sharing one descendant) is fine. ## Build order Subagents are built **leaf-first** (bottom-up): if `A` declares `subAgents: ["B"]` and `B` declares `subAgents: ["C"]`, the generated `GeneratedAgentFactory.bx` builds `C`, then `B` (passing in the built `C` instance), then `A` (passing in the built `B` instance) - never the other way around, since a parent's `aiAgent()` call needs its children's already-built instances. ## Validation * A subagent name in `subAgents` that doesn't correspond to a real `subagents/{name}/` folder (holding an `Agent.yaml` or `Agent.bx`) fails validation with a clear "references unknown subagent \[...\]" error - this applies to **every** node's `subAgents` list, including the root project's own definition, not just nested subagents. * **Circular references** (`A` → `B` → `A`) are rejected at validation time, with the full cycle path reported (e.g. `A -> B -> A`), before any code generation happens. * A "diamond" shape - two subagents both depending on the same shared descendant - is **not** a cycle and builds fine; only genuine cycles are rejected. * A missing `Agent.yaml`/`Agent.bx` inside a discovered `subagents/*` folder is reported as its own validation error, and so is a folder holding both (`BxAgents.AmbiguousAgentDefinition`) - a folder holds one definition. * Every node's own DECLARED `name` (root + every subagent's own definition) must be unique across the whole project - see below. ## Retrieving an agent from `schedules/Scheduler.bx` Two different names are in play, and they're not interchangeable: * The **folder name** under `subagents/` (`researcher` above) is what `subAgents: [ "..." ]` references - it's purely a build-time wiring concern. * The subagent's own **declared `name`** (its agent definition's `name` field, e.g. `"ResearchBot"`) is what you retrieve it by at runtime - every agent in the tree (root + every subagent) is registered in `config/WireBox.bx` under this name, so [`schedules/Scheduler.bx`](/next/conventions/schedules/index.html) (or any other WireBox-aware code) reaches it with a plain `getInstance( "ResearchBot" )`. title: tests/
body: tests/ Every project scaffolded via bxAgents new gets a root box.json (declaring testbox as a development dependency, installed into lib/testbox ) and a ready-to-run tests/ folder with tests/specs/AgentSpec.bx , an example spec that passes out of the box. cd my-agent box install # fetches testbox into lib/testbox (new already ran this for you) bxAgents test Info Inspired by the coldbox-templates/boxlang template's own dedicated tests/ + box.json folder - adapted to BxAgents' own simpler testing story. Testing an agent is about its behavior (what it says, which tools it calls), not HTTP routing, so there's no Application.bx /ColdBox virtual app involved here at all. Writing a spec Extend bxModules.bxagents.models.testing.BaseAgentSpec (a testbox.system.BaseSpec subclass) instead of testbox.system.BaseSpec directly: // tests/specs/AgentSpec.bx class extends="bxModules.bxagents.models.testing.BaseAgentSpec" { function run() { describe( "my-agent", function() { it( "responds to a greeting", function() { mockResponses( [ "Hello! How can I help you today?" ] ) var response = agent.run( "Hi there" ) expect( response ).toContainText( "Hello" ) } ) } ) } } BaseAgentSpec builds your agent once per spec bundle ( beforeAll() ), against a throwaway temp copy of your project - it never touches your real .build/app , so running tests never clobbers (or is clobbered by) a real build / serve / package cycle. The built agent is exposed as agent . Testing against the mock provider By default, bxAgents test builds your agent using the test environment override in Agent.yaml (scaffolded automatically): # Agent.yaml environments: test: model: mock/mock-model A class-based Agent.bx expresses the same override as a test() method returning { model : "mock/mock-model" } . This means your tests need no API key and no network access out of the box - the same mock provider convention used throughout BxAgents' own test suite. Edit this override if you want a spec to run against a real provider instead (you'll need a real API key available in the environment running the tests). mockResponses( responses ) Scripts the agent's next replies, consumed in order - one per LLM round-trip, including the intermediate turns of a tool-calling loop: mockResponses( [ { toolCalls: [ { name: "getWeather", arguments: { city: "Miami" } } ] }, "It's sunny in Miami!" ] ) var response = agent.run( "What's the weather in Miami?" ) A plain string scripts a final reply. A { toolCalls: [ { name, arguments } ] } struct scripts a tool-call turn - the named tool actually executes for real (against your real tools/ implementation), and its real return value is what the next round-trip sees; only the LLM's own reply is scripted, never the tool's behavior. Custom matchers BaseAgentSpec registers a few matchers, tailored to testing agent behavior, via TestBox's own addMatchers() extension point - use them exactly like any built-in TestBox matcher, including negation ( notTo... ): Matcher Checks toContainText( "substring" ) The actual value (usually a response string) contains the given text, case-insensitively. toHaveCalledTool( "toolName" ) The agent's own recorded provider requests show it actually decided to invoke the named tool - not just that the tool exists. toHaveReceivedMessage( "substring" ) Some message actually sent to the provider (any role, any round-trip) contained the given text - useful for asserting your system prompt/instructions actually reached the model. expect( agent ).toHaveCalledTool( "getWeather" ) expect( agent ).notToHaveCalledTool( "getStockPrice" ) Running tests bxAgents test Runs your project's tests/specs/** via TestBox, in a fresh child process (so it never fights over BoxLang's own class-mapping caches with anything else you're running). Prints bundle/suite/spec counts and pass/fail/error/skipped totals, plus one line per failure, and exits non-zero if anything failed - suitable as a CI gate before deploy . Warning bxAgents test requires TestBox actually installed in lib/testbox ( box install in the project root; tests/testbox is also found, for projects scaffolded before box.json moved to the root) - it errors clearly, rather than silently reporting zero specs, if that hasn't been done yet.

# tests/

Every project scaffolded via `bxAgents new` gets a root [`box.json`](/next/conventions/box-json/index.html) (declaring `testbox` as a development dependency, installed into `lib/testbox`) and a ready-to-run `tests/` folder with `tests/specs/AgentSpec.bx`, an example spec that passes out of the box.

```bash
cd my-agent
box install       # fetches testbox into lib/testbox (new already ran this for you)
bxAgents test
```

> **Info**
>
> Inspired by the `coldbox-templates/boxlang` template's own dedicated `tests/` + `box.json` folder - adapted to BxAgents' own simpler testing story. Testing an agent is about its **behavior** (what it says, which tools it calls), not HTTP routing, so there's no `Application.bx`/ColdBox virtual app involved here at all.

## Writing a spec

Extend `bxModules.bxagents.models.testing.BaseAgentSpec` (a `testbox.system.BaseSpec` subclass) instead of `testbox.system.BaseSpec` directly:

```javascript
// tests/specs/AgentSpec.bx
class extends="bxModules.bxagents.models.testing.BaseAgentSpec" {

	function run() {
		describe( "my-agent", function() {

			it( "responds to a greeting", function() {
				mockResponses( [ "Hello! How can I help you today?" ] )

				var response = agent.run( "Hi there" )

				expect( response ).toContainText( "Hello" )
			} )

		} )
	}

}
```

`BaseAgentSpec` builds your agent once per spec bundle (`beforeAll()`), against a **throwaway temp copy** of your project - it never touches your real `.build/app`, so running tests never clobbers (or is clobbered by) a real `build`/`serve`/`package` cycle. The built agent is exposed as `agent`.

## Testing against the mock provider

By default, `bxAgents test` builds your agent using the `test` environment override in `Agent.yaml` (scaffolded automatically):

```yaml
# Agent.yaml
environments:
  test:
    model: mock/mock-model
```

A class-based `Agent.bx` expresses the same override as a `test()` method returning `{ model : "mock/mock-model" }`.

This means your tests need **no API key and no network access** out of the box - the same `mock` provider convention used throughout BxAgents' own test suite. Edit this override if you want a spec to run against a real provider instead (you'll need a real API key available in the environment running the tests).

### `mockResponses( responses )`

Scripts the agent's next replies, consumed in order - one per LLM round-trip, including the intermediate turns of a tool-calling loop:

```javascript
mockResponses( [
	{ toolCalls: [ { name: "getWeather", arguments: { city: "Miami" } } ] },
	"It's sunny in Miami!"
] )

var response = agent.run( "What's the weather in Miami?" )
```

A plain string scripts a final reply. A `{ toolCalls: [ { name, arguments } ] }` struct scripts a tool-call turn - the named tool **actually executes for real** (against your real `tools/` implementation), and its real return value is what the next round-trip sees; only the LLM's own reply is scripted, never the tool's behavior.

## Custom matchers

`BaseAgentSpec` registers a few matchers, tailored to testing agent behavior, via TestBox's own `addMatchers()` extension point - use them exactly like any built-in TestBox matcher, including negation (`notTo...`):

|                Matcher                 |                                                                                      Checks                                                                                       |
|----------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `toContainText( "substring" )`         | The actual value (usually a response string) contains the given text, case-insensitively.                                                                                         |
| `toHaveCalledTool( "toolName" )`       | The agent's own recorded provider requests show it actually decided to invoke the named tool - not just that the tool exists.                                                     |
| `toHaveReceivedMessage( "substring" )` | Some message actually sent to the provider (any role, any round-trip) contained the given text - useful for asserting your system prompt/instructions actually reached the model. |

```javascript
expect( agent ).toHaveCalledTool( "getWeather" )
expect( agent ).notToHaveCalledTool( "getStockPrice" )
```

## Running tests

```bash
bxAgents test
```

Runs your project's `tests/specs/**` via TestBox, in a fresh child process (so it never fights over BoxLang's own class-mapping caches with anything else you're running). Prints bundle/suite/spec counts and pass/fail/error/skipped totals, plus one line per failure, and exits non-zero if anything failed - suitable as a CI gate before `deploy`.
> **Warning**
>
> `bxAgents test` requires TestBox actually installed in `lib/testbox` (`box install` in the project root; `tests/testbox` is also found, for projects scaffolded before `box.json` moved to the root) - it errors clearly, rather than silently reporting zero specs, if that hasn't been done yet.
